sections.html:
Given a trading description, identify when terms are fixed, compare future spot/forward/futures, choose a matching offset, count open interest without double counting, explain clearing and the broker warning, and distinguish maturity settlement, daily price limits and position limits. This is a coherent capability to explain what contractual obligation a trader opens and how it ends; it does not assess legal rules or current exchange specifications.

Study conditions, assessment scope and sources

Finished-note locations: When the agreement, payment and delivery happen; Standardized futures specifications; Positions, open interest and the clearing house; How the obligation ends; Trading limits and market abuse; Problem 1: offsetting contracts.

Supported learning permits these note sections and the worked key. Independent checks permit blank paper and a non-programmable calculator only; no notes, formula list, key, hints, external help or generated solution. The tutor must confirm these conditions and known prior item exposure before marking independence. Unknown conditions are unscorable for independence, even if the content is correct. These stricter practice conditions do not purport to reproduce all exam rules. Hypothetical tasks below instantiate only note-supported mechanisms.

Check the prerequisites

No earlier course objective is required. O001-P0 / v1: A buyer intends today to buy in December but will agree the price only in December. Is today's price fixed? Key: no; intention is future spot, all specification/payment/delivery belong to the future deal. Pass: identifies unfixed future price and why; partial: correct label without timing; fail: says intention fixes it. Repair: the first two paragraphs of Explanation steps, then W1. This is an entry diagnostic of the objective, not an external assumed foundation.

A qualifying committed prerequisite result may skip its diagnostic only when its exact current tuple or explicitly approved compatible tuple and independence conditions are known. Familiarity is insufficient. Diagnostics do not count as acquisition checks. Do each relevant diagnostic once; failed/partial responses follow the stated repair, then one fresh full check rather than repeated diagnosis.
sections.title: Prerequisites and checks

sections.html: Motivation: How can a later purchase have terms fixed today, and how can an obligation disappear before delivery? Spot agrees the current-price trade now, permitting the note's practical settlement delay. Future spot waits to trade at the later then-current price. A forward privately specifies asset, quantity, price and maturity now, with payment/delivery later. Futures standardize exchange terms, add clearing and daily settlement. Long means bought, short means sold. Open interest counts contracts via either open longs or open shorts, not their sum. Grade, delivery location and month matter to contract identity. The course's usual financial months and illustrative delivery percentages are introductory source statements, not universal live facts.
sections.title: Motivation, intuition, and definitions

sections.html:
1. Separate specifying the deal from performing it: later delivery alone does not show whether price was agreed now. A forward supplies today's terms; waiting supplies none.
  2. A fixed price removes that agreed-price uncertainty but creates unfavorable-value incentives to default: above the forward price the seller prefers spot; below it the buyer prefers spot.
  3. Published asset, size, grade, place and delivery month make futures interchangeable. An equal opposite position in the same contract offsets; an opposite different month leaves two obligations.
  4. Clearing interposes a formal counterparty and tracks/net positions through members, reducing reliance on the original opposing client. Brokers remain the client's access path. The notes explicitly warn about own-broker default; the handout's contrary wording is unresolved, so do not claim unlimited protection.
  5. Offset before maturity ends open delivery exposure and fixes cumulative trading result. At maturity physical settlement delivers an eligible asset against cash (notification, assignment, eligible delivery, invoice/payment); cash settlement uses the defined final reference EDSP. An eligible-asset choice can permit cheapest-to-deliver selection; later bond calculations are excluded.
  6. A daily price limit constrains the session band around prior settlement and may suspend trading; a position limit constrains speculative concentration. Neither is a lifetime loss guarantee. Cornering combines concentrated long futures with control of underlying supply, hurting shorts' ability to close/deliver. Margin supports performance and does not buy the asset.

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Spot, forward and futures contracts; fingerprint ed4177199ebe557e2c52129bcd94b690b22e553a5eafba9ce5f4dc19656c3045. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Spot, forward and futures contracts

How can a trader agree today on an exchange that will occur later, and what makes that agreement reliable? Week 1 separates price agreement from payment and delivery. A forward fixes a later exchange through a private agreement; a futures contract adds exchange standardization, clearing and daily settlement. These arrangements explain both the usefulness of futures for managing price uncertainty and the cash obligations a trader accepts. L10(EssentialsOfFuturesTrading).pptx, slide 2–5 FI01(Futures Contracts).doc, Ch. I, LibreOffice-rendered p. 2–4

Topic map

The map synthesizes the selected handout chapter: classification on pp. 2–3, clearing and margins on pp. 3–5, convergence on p. 6, hedging on p. 7 and payoff/limits on pp. 8–9. It describes the Week 1 mechanism; it does not import the later chapters on financial contract examples, cost of carry or trading strategies. FI01(Futures Contracts).doc, Ch. I, LibreOffice-rendered p. 2–9

When the agreement, payment and delivery happen

A spot contract agrees an immediate sale and delivery at the current spot, or prompt, price. The lecture allows the usual practical delay of up to two days between transaction and settlement; the defining point is that the deal uses the price prevailing now. A future spot contract, in the lecture's terminology, means waiting until a specified future date to make a spot transaction. Its future price is still unknown today. Merely intending to buy later does not fix a price. L10(EssentialsOfFuturesTrading).pptx, slide 2 FI01(Futures Contracts).doc, Ch. I, LibreOffice-rendered p. 2

Source timelines: S means specification, P payment, and D delivery. The upper line places all three near the present; the lower line postpones all three to the future date T. The lower transaction therefore retains future spot-price uncertainty. L10(EssentialsOfFuturesTrading).pptx, slide 2

A forward contract specifies today the underlying asset and quantity, the agreed forward price, and the future delivery or maturity date. Payment and delivery occur later. The parties can tailor these terms to their business needs. The benefit is that the agreed exchange price is known in advance. The cost is that a unique private obligation may be difficult or expensive to transfer or terminate. L10(EssentialsOfFuturesTrading).pptx, slide 3 FI01(Futures Contracts).doc, Ch. I, LibreOffice-rendered p. 2

The forward timeline places S at the beginning and P and D at T: fixing the terms and executing the exchange are separate events. L10(EssentialsOfFuturesTrading).pptx, slide 3

Fixing a price also creates an incentive for the losing party to default. If the later spot price \(S\) exceeds the agreed price \(F\), the buyer prefers delivery at \(F\), while the seller could obtain more by selling at \(S\). If \(S\) is below \(F\), the seller prefers the agreement, while the buyer would prefer to buy spot. This is a credit-risk problem arising from an obligation's unfavorable market value, even though the contract has removed uncertainty about the agreed price. L10(EssentialsOfFuturesTrading).pptx, slide 3 FI01(Futures Contracts).doc, Ch. I, LibreOffice-rendered p. 2

Standardized futures specifications

A futures contract is a standardized agreement for a future exchange, traded on a specialized exchange. The trader accepts the published terms and chooses whether to buy or sell at the available futures price. Standardization makes contracts comparable and allows an opposite trade to unwind a position. The lecture presents this ease of offsetting as an important source of liquidity. L10(EssentialsOfFuturesTrading).pptx, slide 4, 7 FI01(Futures Contracts).doc, Ch. I, LibreOffice-rendered p. 2–3 02_seminar.pdf, PDF p. 3

A futures contract is a derivative because its price is derived from the underlying asset's price. The specifications identify the underlying asset, contract size, delivery month, quotation and minimum price movement, and delivery arrangements. An underlying asset may be a commodity, an index, an equity, a currency or an interest-rate-related instrument. For commodities, the grade of quality matters because goods of different quality need not have the same price. Delivery location also matters when transport costs are significant; alternative locations can require price adjustments. 02_seminar.pdf, PDF p. 3–4 02_seminar.pdf, PDF p. 8

The contract multiplier converts a quoted price movement into a monetary gain or loss. If a price is quoted in dollars per barrel and the contract covers 1,000 barrels, a $0.01 rise per barrel changes the contract's monetary value by $10. If an index contract pays $50 per index point and its minimum movement is 0.25 points, one tick is $12.50. In both cases,

\[\text{tick value}=\text{tick size}\times\text{contract multiplier}.\]

The units must cancel correctly: dollars per barrel times barrels gives dollars; index points times dollars per point gives dollars. For \(N\) contracts, multiply the monetary change by \(N\). These are the seminar's examples, rather than claims that every oil or index contract uses those specifications. 02_seminar.pdf, PDF p. 5

The seminar's fractional quotation example is \(99+21.75/32=99.6796875\), or approximately 99.68, for the written quote \(99\text{-}21\tfrac34\). Its text first discusses Treasury bonds and then labels the example “US T-Bill”; the label is internally inconsistent, so the verified learning point here is the arithmetic of the fractional quote. 02_seminar.pdf, PDF p. 7

The seminar describes usual maturities as ranging from one month to two years. This is its introductory description; a particular contract's published terms determine its available maturities. 02_seminar.pdf, PDF p. 6

Delivery month is part of the contract's identity: a June contract and a September contract are different obligations. The lecture and seminar describe March, June, September and December as usual financial-contract months, and the seminar says commodity contracts may be available monthly. These are the supplied introductory descriptions; the specified contract calendar remains necessary for an actual contract. A contract that is too large can exclude smaller traders, while one that is too small increases the number of transactions needed for a desired exposure. L10(EssentialsOfFuturesTrading).pptx, slide 4 FI01(Futures Contracts).doc, Ch. I, LibreOffice-rendered p. 3 02_seminar.pdf, PDF p. 6

Positions, open interest and the clearing house

A long position is a bought futures contract; a short position is a sold futures contract. Each outstanding contract has a long and a short side. Open interest counts the outstanding contracts as the number of open longs or, equivalently, open shorts; it does not add both sides and double-count the same contracts. L10(EssentialsOfFuturesTrading).pptx, slide 5

The clearing arrangement places the exchange or clearing house between the original counterparties after brokers arrange the trade. The clearing house keeps track of transactions and becomes the formal counterparty, honoring the agreed obligations within the arrangement described by the sources. Non-members channel their trades through members, and the clearing house calculates members' net positions. This reduces the trader's exposure to the original opposing client. L10(EssentialsOfFuturesTrading).pptx, slide 12 FI01(Futures Contracts).doc, Ch. I, LibreOffice-rendered p. 3 02_seminar.pdf, PDF p. 11

Compare the direct relationship above with the interposed exchange below. The intermediate counterparty changes whom each side relies on for the agreed transaction; brokers still connect clients to the exchange. L10(EssentialsOfFuturesTrading).pptx, slide 12

The lecture explicitly says this arrangement does not protect a client against the default of their own broker. The handout p. 3 contains both a sentence about honoring obligations after a broker's default and this same non-protection warning. Those statements should be retained as a source ambiguity rather than turned into a blanket guarantee that clients cannot lose money through a broker. The diagram establishes the interposition of clearing; it does not establish unlimited protection against every participant's default. L10(EssentialsOfFuturesTrading).pptx, slide 12 FI01(Futures Contracts).doc, Ch. I, LibreOffice-rendered p. 3

How the obligation ends

Closing out means taking an offsetting position in an equivalent contract before maturity. A long sells the same underlying, contract size and delivery-month contract; a short buys it. The offset removes the open delivery obligation and fixes the cumulative trading result. A sale in a different delivery month would leave exposure in another contract rather than provide the matching offset. L10(EssentialsOfFuturesTrading).pptx, slide 7 FI01(Futures Contracts).doc, Ch. I, LibreOffice-rendered p. 5 02_seminar.pdf, PDF p. 9

A position held to maturity follows its specified settlement method. Physical delivery exchanges the eligible underlying asset and cash. The source sequence is a long's notification, clearing-house assignment of a short, delivery of an eligible asset and determination/payment of the invoice. If the contract permits several eligible assets, the handout introduces the short's cheapest-to-deliver choice without developing the later bond calculations. Cash settlement transfers the final monetary amount when delivery is impractical, costly or excluded by the specification. The final marking-to-market price is the Exchange Delivery Settlement Price (EDSP). L10(EssentialsOfFuturesTrading).pptx, slide 7 FI01(Futures Contracts).doc, Ch. I, LibreOffice-rendered p. 5 02_seminar.pdf, PDF p. 8–9

The seminar states that less than 1% of all futures contracts end in commodity delivery and emphasizes that most traders offset. Treat that percentage as the seminar's illustrative statement; it supplies no sample, date or measurement method. The broader source-supported point is that closing out is common and enables trading without arranging physical delivery. 02_seminar.pdf, PDF p. 9 L10(EssentialsOfFuturesTrading).pptx, slide 7

Trading limits and market abuse

Daily price limits define a permitted band around the previous day's settlement price. The handout describes limit-up or limit-down suspension when prices pass that band, with a cooling-off period intended to help participants reassess positions. Position limits cap the number of speculative contracts one trader, or a coordinated group, can hold. These limits constrain market influence rather than specifying a maximum possible loss on a position. FI01(Futures Contracts).doc, Ch. I, LibreOffice-rendered p. 8 02_seminar.pdf, PDF p. 14

The handout describes cornering the market as combining many long futures positions with control of the underlying supply, raising the underlying price and making it difficult for shorts to close or deliver at a reasonable price. This explains why position limits address concentration as well as the leverage created by small margin deposits. FI01(Futures Contracts).doc, Ch. I, LibreOffice-rendered p. 8

What to carry forward

The essential tradeoff is between a negotiated future exchange and a standardized obligation that can be offset and cleared. Standardization supports liquidity; clearing and daily settlement address counterparty exposure; margin makes the obligation operational but does not pay for the asset or cap its loss. The next note, Margins and marking to market, explains the daily cash mechanism. Basis, convergence and futures hedging shows why combining that mechanism with a spot transaction fixes a price only under the stated matching and convergence conditions. L10(EssentialsOfFuturesTrading).pptx, slide 4–10

Origin: reused complete checked passage Problem 1: offsetting contracts; fingerprint b10a0ed1ddfde242583a447a4246738dc8f31af4dca1c5f77970596782335d04. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Problem 1: offsetting contracts

John buys ten June Nasdaq 100 futures contracts on 9 January and wants to close them on 16 April. He sells ten equivalent June Nasdaq 100 contracts on 16 April. Matching the underlying, delivery month and number cancels his existing long position; daily settlement fixes his cumulative gain/loss as ten times the multiplier times closing minus opening futures price. Jane opens a short September S&P 500 contract in early August and closes it a week later by buying one equivalent September S&P 500 contract. A contract of another maturity would create a different position rather than be the matching offset. The question supplies no opening or closing prices, so it cannot determine a numerical profit. 02_seminar.pdf, PDF p. 17 L10(EssentialsOfFuturesTrading).pptx, slide 6–7

Course organization

The supplied 2026/2027 handbook and SIS export identify this course as JEM035, worth 6 ECTS, with English instruction. Its scope concerns futures and options and their use in speculative, hedging and arbitrage trading; the summer course Financial Markets Instruments II is the continuation. The existing descriptive course-folder name is retained. The futures/options syllabus provides course context; later topics have not been turned into teaching notes by this Week 1 pass. handbook-1.pdf, PDF p. 1–3 Předměty.pdf, PDF p. 1–2

Teaching and communication

As of the handbook's 29 September 2026 update, the lecture is Tuesday 14:00–15:20 in room 314 and the seminar Tuesday 15:30–16:50 in room 109. In-person attendance is recommended, not mandatory. Lecture questions go to Prof. Oldřich Dědek, and seminar/exam questions to Petr Polák; the handbook recommends asking in person and specifies dedek@fsv.cuni.cz and petr.polak@fsv.cuni.cz, with an email subject beginning “FMI I:”. These are recorded source arrangements, not live schedule verification or messages sent by the assistant. handbook-1.pdf, PDF p. 1–2

The SIS export also supplies a Teams invitation/code under its English teaching-methods section and directs grading questions to the handbook. Its administrative interface and historical enrollment/results table on pp. 2–3 do not establish academic concepts or the learner's own performance. The external Teams/lecturer links and recommended books are not additional sources read in this pass. Předměty.pdf, PDF p. 2–3

Assessment and the handbook's cutoff ambiguity

The handbook allocates 20 points to seminar activity and 80 to the written exam. At least 50% of the final exam, hence 40 out of 80, is needed for eligibility to pass. It says there are three attempts and that an exam score cannot be improved after the minimum requirement has been passed. It also says at least 50 total points are needed; however, its grade table labels 0–50 as F and starts E at 51. The exact treatment of a total of 50 is therefore unresolved in the supplied handbook and should be clarified with the teaching assistant; it is not silently chosen here. The table gives E=51–60, D=61–70, C=71–80, B=81–90 and A=91–100. handbook-1.pdf, PDF p. 3–4

Seminars begin with a brief theory recap and around three worked board exercises, then allow roughly 15–20 minutes for a point-bearing problem. The handbook gives up to three points per seminar, capped at 20 overall, and asks students to bring the formula list and a calculator. Question sets are supplied in SIS, while solutions are not. The written exam includes 40 theory points and four exercises worth 10 each; full exercise credit requires careful steps and explanation. handbook-1.pdf, PDF p. 4

Only a non-programmable calculator is allowed in the exam. The handbook prohibits communication devices, books, own notes, teamwork and exchange of notes, and says the formula list will be provided. SIS registration is compulsory. handbook-1.pdf, PDF p. 4–5

Listed examination dates and materials

The handbook lists 15 December 2026, 5 January 2027 and 19 January 2027, each 15:30–16:50. It assigns O314 to the December date and leaves the January rooms unknown, explicitly noting that times and rooms can change. It also discusses an exam in the last seminar; no unlisted additional date is invented from that sentence. These are the uploaded handbook's dates, not a checked live calendar. handbook-1.pdf, PDF p. 5

The handbook lists presentations and handouts plus books by Blake, Hull, Björk and Jílek and the Black–Scholes paper as available/recommended literature. The SIS export lists earlier editions and describes its linked Handbook.pdf as 2025/2026, whereas the actual uploaded handbook-1.pdf cover states 2026/2027. Those labels are preserved as a provenance difference. They do not authorize opening external websites or extending Week 1 into options pricing or the remaining futures chapters. handbook-1.pdf, PDF p. 1, 5 Předměty.pdf, PDF p. 1–2

O001-W1 / item_version 1 / worked-example; source-supported example or explicitly hypothetical instantiation.

John buys ten June Nasdaq futures and closes in April by selling ten equivalent June contracts. Selling September instead would create a September short while leaving the June long. Jane shorts one September S&P contract and closes by buying one equivalent September contract. These are the note's source exercises; no numerical profit follows without opening/closing prices. If ten outstanding contracts have ten long and ten short sides, open interest is ten. Decision checks: contract month and size match; opposite direction alone is insufficient. Clearing does not erase own-broker risk. Held positions follow physical/cash specification; an offset ends the open delivery obligation.

Prompt: A bakery will buy grain in December. Compare (a) waiting to negotiate then, (b) privately fixing price/quantity today, and (c) buying standardized December futures today. sections.title: Motivation, intuition, and definitions

sections.html:
1. Convert every quote to the units matched by \(q\). Dollars per pound times pounds gives dollars.
  2. A long earns \(Nq(F_{\mathrm{close}}-F_{\mathrm{open}})\); a short earns \(Nq(F_{\mathrm{open}}-F_{\mathrm{close}})\). Opposite sides sum to zero for the same inputs.
  3. Daily differences telescope, so cumulative payoff uses endpoints for a fixed position; at maturity replace closing \(F\) by \(S\) only under convergence. Break-even is \(\text{final price}=F_{\mathrm{open}}\); long slope +\(Nq\) and short −\(Nq\).
  4. Margin is the trader's deposit, not a payoff ceiling or asset price. With \(F\ge 0\), a long's maximum loss is \(NqF_{\mathrm{open}}\) at zero. If no lower bound exists this finite maximum is not established. With no upper bound, short loss is unbounded. Price/position limits likewise do not truncate the payoff line.
  5. A changed number example is a parallel calculation, not proof of broad transfer. Keep given price-bound assumptions visible in the answer.
sections.title: Explanation steps

sections.html:
Reading context

Deliver these complete reused passages before the worked example; the earlier concise teaching prompts are checkpoints, not substitutes. Necessary prerequisite lessons remain the routes specified above. Course-organization details in O001 are supporting context, not additional scoring components.

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Standardized futures specifications; fingerprint ed4177199ebe557e2c52129bcd94b690b22e553a5eafba9ce5f4dc19656c3045. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Standardized futures specifications

A futures contract is a standardized agreement for a future exchange, traded on a specialized exchange. The trader accepts the published terms and chooses whether to buy or sell at the available futures price. Standardization makes contracts comparable and allows an opposite trade to unwind a position. The lecture presents this ease of offsetting as an important source of liquidity. L10(EssentialsOfFuturesTrading).pptx, slide 4, 7 FI01(Futures Contracts).doc, Ch. I, LibreOffice-rendered p. 2–3 02_seminar.pdf, PDF p. 3

A futures contract is a derivative because its price is derived from the underlying asset's price. The specifications identify the underlying asset, contract size, delivery month, quotation and minimum price movement, and delivery arrangements. An underlying asset may be a commodity, an index, an equity, a currency or an interest-rate-related instrument. For commodities, the grade of quality matters because goods of different quality need not have the same price. Delivery location also matters when transport costs are significant; alternative locations can require price adjustments. 02_seminar.pdf, PDF p. 3–4 02_seminar.pdf, PDF p. 8

The contract multiplier converts a quoted price movement into a monetary gain or loss. If a price is quoted in dollars per barrel and the contract covers 1,000 barrels, a $0.01 rise per barrel changes the contract's monetary value by $10. If an index contract pays $50 per index point and its minimum movement is 0.25 points, one tick is $12.50. In both cases,

\[\text{tick value}=\text{tick size}\times\text{contract multiplier}.\]

The units must cancel correctly: dollars per barrel times barrels gives dollars; index points times dollars per point gives dollars. For \(N\) contracts, multiply the monetary change by \(N\). These are the seminar's examples, rather than claims that every oil or index contract uses those specifications. 02_seminar.pdf, PDF p. 5

The seminar's fractional quotation example is \(99+21.75/32=99.6796875\), or approximately 99.68, for the written quote \(99\text{-}21\tfrac34\). Its text first discusses Treasury bonds and then labels the example “US T-Bill”; the label is internally inconsistent, so the verified learning point here is the arithmetic of the fractional quote. 02_seminar.pdf, PDF p. 7

The seminar describes usual maturities as ranging from one month to two years. This is its introductory description; a particular contract's published terms determine its available maturities. 02_seminar.pdf, PDF p. 6

Delivery month is part of the contract's identity: a June contract and a September contract are different obligations. The lecture and seminar describe March, June, September and December as usual financial-contract months, and the seminar says commodity contracts may be available monthly. These are the supplied introductory descriptions; the specified contract calendar remains necessary for an actual contract. A contract that is too large can exclude smaller traders, while one that is too small increases the number of transactions needed for a desired exposure. L10(EssentialsOfFuturesTrading).pptx, slide 4 FI01(Futures Contracts).doc, Ch. I, LibreOffice-rendered p. 3 02_seminar.pdf, PDF p. 6

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Daily profit and loss, with units; fingerprint c92b574f4c33c97bdbefad673c63cc8029a344a79d7b1da69ed2bba44076e313. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Daily profit and loss, with units

Let \(F_0\) be the opening futures price, \(F_t\) the settlement price at the end of day t, \(N\) the number of contracts and \(q\) the multiplier converting one quoted price unit into money per contract. With a constant position size and multiplier,

\[G_t^{\mathrm{long}}=Nq(F_t-F_{t-1}),\qquad G_t^{\mathrm{short}}=Nq(F_{t-1}-F_t)=-G_t^{\mathrm{long}}.\]

A price rise credits the long and debits the short; a fall reverses these transfers. The lecture writes the price difference for a normalized unit; \(Nq\) restores the contract units used by the seminar's tick examples. For a commodity quoted in dollars per pound, \(q\) is pounds per contract. For a contract quoted directly in dollars per contract, \(q=1\). L10(EssentialsOfFuturesTrading).pptx, slide 6 FI01(Futures Contracts).doc, Ch. I, LibreOffice-rendered p. 4–5 02_seminar.pdf, PDF p. 5, 12

Adding the daily transfers cancels every intermediate price:

\[\sum_{t=1}^{k}G_t^{\mathrm{long}} =Nq\big[(F_1-F_0)+(F_2-F_1)+\cdots +(F_k-F_{k-1})\big] =Nq(F_k-F_0).\]

The short obtains the opposite amount. This telescoping sum explains why the total trading result equals the closing minus opening price, even though it is paid in installments. The account can require cash along the way even when the final cumulative result is favorable. The source's reasoning ignores interest earned or paid on the timing of settlement cash flows. L10(EssentialsOfFuturesTrading).pptx, slide 6 FI01(Futures Contracts).doc, Ch. I, LibreOffice-rendered p. 7

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Payoff and the size of possible losses; fingerprint c92b574f4c33c97bdbefad673c63cc8029a344a79d7b1da69ed2bba44076e313. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Payoff and the size of possible losses

For a position held to maturity with \(F_T=S_T\), cumulative trading results are

\[\Pi_T^{\mathrm{long}}=Nq(S_T-F_0),\qquad \Pi_T^{\mathrm{short}}=Nq(F_0-S_T).\]

They have equal magnitude and opposite signs. A long benefits from a higher final underlying price; a short benefits from a lower one. The source diagram crosses zero at \(S_T=F_0\) and shows linear results on either side. Margin does not truncate either line. FI01(Futures Contracts).doc, Ch. I, LibreOffice-rendered p. 7–8 L10(EssentialsOfFuturesTrading).pptx, slide 11

The horizontal axis is the maturity spot price \(S_T\). The long line slopes upward and the short line downward; their common break-even point is the opening futures price \(F_0\). The vertical direction represents gain/loss, not the margin account balance. FI01(Futures Contracts).doc, Ch. I, LibreOffice-rendered p. 8

A claimed maximum long loss needs a lower bound on the price. If the modeled final price cannot go below zero, the maximum loss is \(NqF_0\) at zero. If the problem imposes no lower bound, that particular finite maximum does not follow from the payoff formula. With no upper price bound, a short's theoretical loss has no finite maximum. These are algebraic consequences of the source payoff, and the required assumptions are made explicit in the copper exercise. FI01(Futures Contracts).doc, Ch. I, LibreOffice-rendered p. 8 02_seminar.pdf, PDF p. 19

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Problem 3: copper and maximum loss; fingerprint b10a0ed1ddfde242583a447a4246738dc8f31af4dca1c5f77970596782335d04. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Problem 3: copper and maximum loss

One long November contract covers 25,000 pounds at $0.78 per pound. Its normalized cumulative result at a closing/settlement price \(F\) is

\[\Pi^{\mathrm{long}}=25000(F-0.78).\]

If one additionally assumes \(F\) cannot be negative, the largest loss is \(25000\times0.78=\$19,500\), reached at \(F=0\). The question itself does not state a lower price bound, so \(19,500\) is a conditional result rather than a bound implied by futures margin. If the model admits arbitrarily negative \(F\), the long formula has no finite loss bound. For the short, \(\Pi^{\mathrm{short}}=25000(0.78-F)\): with no upper price bound, an arbitrarily high \(F\) gives an arbitrarily large loss. The initial margin is never a maximum-loss guarantee. 02_seminar.pdf, PDF p. 19 FI01(Futures Contracts).doc, Ch. I, LibreOffice-rendered p. 8

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage The seminar's film illustration; fingerprint b10a0ed1ddfde242583a447a4246738dc8f31af4dca1c5f77970596782335d04. Heading depth alone is adapted.

The seminar's film illustration

Page 15 supplies a short-trade illustration: 450,000 pounds sold at $1.42 and bought back at $0.29, a difference of $1.13 per pound. Its multiplication is \(450000\times1.13=\$508,500\), corresponding to 30 contracts of 15,000 pounds each. This is the supplied illustration's trading gain before costs, not an explanation of its margin-account path. The PDF also contains external video links and the phrase “Eddie Murphy Rule”; the selected slide does not define the rule, and the videos were not opened. No legal claim is inferred from that label. 02_seminar.pdf, PDF p. 15

For one long 18,000-lb contract at 65 cents with \(F\ge 0\), give maximum loss; then remove the lower bound and discuss a short without an upper bound and why an initial deposit does not settle that question.
interactions.solution_html: Key and essential rubric: Exposure \(2\times\$40=\$80/\text{point}\). Short \(80(1800-1807)=-\$560\); opposite long +$560. Tick \(0.5\times 80=\$40\) per position tick. Break-even \(1800\) points; short payoff slopes downward and long payoff upward. Fraction \(103+10.25/32=103.3203125\); \(65\text{ cents}=\$0.65\). For the separate nonnegative-price long, maximum loss is \(18,000\times 0.65=\$11,700\) at zero. Removing the lower price bound removes that finite bound; absence of an upper price bound makes short loss unbounded. Initial deposit is separate funding and cannot bound the price-based payoff. All three components and their stated assumptions/units are required.

sections.title: Prerequisites and checks

sections.html: Motivation: A profitable final trade can still demand cash on earlier days. \(I\) is initial deposit, \(M\) maintenance minimum, \(R\) stated restoration target, \(G\) daily signed \(\mathrm{P/L}\), \(A^{-}\) pre-adjustment balance, \(C\) top-up and \(W\) withdrawal. \(A^{-}=\text{previous }A+G\); if \(A^-<M\), \(C=R-A^{-}\); otherwise \(C=0\); \(A=A^{-}+C-W\). Equality with \(M\) is no call under this strict rule. Both sides deposit initial margin. Leverage means a full-contract movement can be large relative to initial deposit. The source's 5–15% illustration is not a universal requirement. Variation margin can name daily settlement transfers or additional deposits; record \(G\) and \(C\) separately.
sections.title: Motivation, intuition, and definitions

sections.html:
1. Use adjacent settlement prices to compute \(G_{\mathrm{long}}=Nq(F_t-F_{\mathrm{previous}})\), \(G_{\mathrm{short}}\) opposite. Both \(N\) and \(q\) must remain fixed; changing positions belongs to O005.
  2. Add \(G\) to previous ending account before funding. Compare this \(A^{-}\) with \(M\).
  3. Only after a breach compute \(R-A^{-}\). Initial and maintenance restoration produce different balances and deposits but identical trading result. Do not silently choose a target when none is given.
  4. Withdraw only under stated retained-balance policy. A deposit is cash funding; a withdrawal is cash removal; neither is a trade gain/loss.
  5. Sum \(G\): middle prices cancel, giving \(Nq(F_{\mathrm{final}}-F_{\mathrm{open}})\) for a long. Reconcile \(\mathrm{P/L}=A_{\mathrm{final}}+\text{total withdrawals}-\text{total deposits}\) (including initial).
  6. A missed call can trigger forced reverse trade at trader cost. Funding along the path remains necessary even when final \(\mathrm{P/L}\) is favorable. This is why a final payoff calculation alone is not a liquidity plan.
sections.title: Explanation steps

sections.html:
Reading context

Deliver these complete reused passages before the worked example; the earlier concise teaching prompts are checkpoints, not substitutes. Necessary prerequisite lessons remain the routes specified above. Course-organization details in O001 are supporting context, not additional scoring components.

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage The three margin concepts; fingerprint c92b574f4c33c97bdbefad673c63cc8029a344a79d7b1da69ed2bba44076e313. Heading depth alone is adapted.

The three margin concepts

Initial margin, \(I\), is the required deposit when opening a position. Both the long and short must post it. The lecture says it is the trader's money in the margin account, not the price paid for the underlying asset. Because it is only a fraction of the underlying contract value, it creates leverage: a given movement in the full contract's price can be large relative to this initial deposit. The seminar gives 5–15% as a usual illustrative range rather than a universal required rate. L10(EssentialsOfFuturesTrading).pptx, slide 5 FI01(Futures Contracts).doc, Ch. I, LibreOffice-rendered p. 4 02_seminar.pdf, PDF p. 11

Maintenance margin, \(M\), is the minimum allowed account balance. Daily losses may reduce the balance below \(M\). A margin call is then a notice to restore the balance to the specified target. The lecture allows a target of maintenance or initial margin; the handout describes restoring maintenance; the seminar's formula uses initial margin. The target must therefore be stated when doing calculations. L10(EssentialsOfFuturesTrading).pptx, slide 5 FI01(Futures Contracts).doc, Ch. I, LibreOffice-rendered p. 4 02_seminar.pdf, PDF p. 13

The lecture and handout call the extra deposited funds variation margin. The seminar also uses that phrase for the daily transfer of settlement gains/losses and writes “\(\text{Variation Margin}=\text{Initial Margin}-\text{Margin balance}\).” That expression describes a top-up to initial margin when the balance is deficient; it is not a formula saying every daily settlement payment equals \(I\) minus the balance. These meanings share the aim of limiting unpaid losses, but use different cash-account conventions. Below, “daily gain/loss” means the price-based transfer and “top-up” means the additional deposit after a call. L10(EssentialsOfFuturesTrading).pptx, slide 5–6 FI01(Futures Contracts).doc, Ch. I, LibreOffice-rendered p. 4 02_seminar.pdf, PDF p. 12–13

The seminar describes maintenance both as a minimum balance and as a payment made after adverse movement. The minimum is the threshold; the required payment is the amount needed to restore the chosen target. Keeping these quantities separate prevents confusing a $2,000 threshold with a $2,000 deposit in every case. 02_seminar.pdf, PDF p. 13

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Daily profit and loss, with units; fingerprint c92b574f4c33c97bdbefad673c63cc8029a344a79d7b1da69ed2bba44076e313. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Daily profit and loss, with units

Let \(F_0\) be the opening futures price, \(F_t\) the settlement price at the end of day t, \(N\) the number of contracts and \(q\) the multiplier converting one quoted price unit into money per contract. With a constant position size and multiplier,

\[G_t^{\mathrm{long}}=Nq(F_t-F_{t-1}),\qquad G_t^{\mathrm{short}}=Nq(F_{t-1}-F_t)=-G_t^{\mathrm{long}}.\]

A price rise credits the long and debits the short; a fall reverses these transfers. The lecture writes the price difference for a normalized unit; \(Nq\) restores the contract units used by the seminar's tick examples. For a commodity quoted in dollars per pound, \(q\) is pounds per contract. For a contract quoted directly in dollars per contract, \(q=1\). L10(EssentialsOfFuturesTrading).pptx, slide 6 FI01(Futures Contracts).doc, Ch. I, LibreOffice-rendered p. 4–5 02_seminar.pdf, PDF p. 5, 12

Adding the daily transfers cancels every intermediate price:

\[\sum_{t=1}^{k}G_t^{\mathrm{long}} =Nq\big[(F_1-F_0)+(F_2-F_1)+\cdots +(F_k-F_{k-1})\big] =Nq(F_k-F_0).\]

The short obtains the opposite amount. This telescoping sum explains why the total trading result equals the closing minus opening price, even though it is paid in installments. The account can require cash along the way even when the final cumulative result is favorable. The source's reasoning ignores interest earned or paid on the timing of settlement cash flows. L10(EssentialsOfFuturesTrading).pptx, slide 6 FI01(Futures Contracts).doc, Ch. I, LibreOffice-rendered p. 7

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage From daily result to an account balance; fingerprint c92b574f4c33c97bdbefad673c63cc8029a344a79d7b1da69ed2bba44076e313. Heading depth alone is adapted.

From daily result to an account balance

Let \(A_{t-1}\) be the previous ending account balance. Before any top-up or withdrawal, the new balance is

\[A_t^- = A_{t-1}+G_t.\]

If a call restores a target \(R\), the deposit is \(C_t=R-A_t^-\) when \(A_t^-<M\); otherwise there is no call. With a withdrawal \(W_t\), the ending balance becomes

\[A_t=A_t^-+C_t-W_t.\]

These equations are an explicit accounting synthesis of the source descriptions. A deposit increases the balance but does not create trading profit; a withdrawal decreases the balance but does not create trading loss. If a trader fails to meet a call, the exchange/clearing house can close the position through a reverse trade at that trader's cost. L10(EssentialsOfFuturesTrading).pptx, slide 5–6 FI01(Futures Contracts).doc, Ch. I, LibreOffice-rendered p. 4 02_seminar.pdf, PDF p. 12–13

The handout's five-day example

The complete source table has an opening price of 1,000 and both initial and maintenance margin equal to 200. Closing prices are 1,100, 1,200, 1,050, 950 and 900. The source uses a one-unit price-to-money normalization. FI01(Futures Contracts).doc, Ch. I, LibreOffice-rendered p. 9

The long receives 100 on each of the first two days, then loses 150, 100 and 50. Its cumulative gain/loss is therefore 100, 200, 50, −50 and −100. On day 4 the balance falls from 250 to 150 and a deposit of 50 restores it to 200. On day 5 the balance again needs 50. The long ends with 200 in the account after depositing 100 beyond its initial 200, but its trading result is −100. The account balance is not its profit. FI01(Futures Contracts).doc, Ch. I, LibreOffice-rendered p. 9

The short loses 100 on each of the first two days and posts 100 each time to restore 200. It then gains 150, 100 and 50, ending with 500. Total deposits were 400, so the account's net surplus over deposits is 100, equal to its trading gain. This compares the two positions' opposite cash transfers and illustrates why small initial deposits can require substantial later funding. FI01(Futures Contracts).doc, Ch. I, LibreOffice-rendered p. 9

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Problem 4: a daily margin table; fingerprint b10a0ed1ddfde242583a447a4246738dc8f31af4dca1c5f77970596782335d04. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Problem 4: a daily margin table

There are 20 long contracts quoted directly in dollars per contract, with prices 82, 84, 78, 81 and 79. Total initial margin is \(20\times5=100\) and total maintenance is \(20\times2=40\). The original blank table is retained because its settlement-price column is visual content absent from native text extraction. 02_seminar.pdf, PDF p. 20

Source table: day 0 is the opening at 82; days 1–4 settle at 84, 78, 81 and 79. The table requests opening balance, deposits, price change, gain/loss and ending balance. 02_seminar.pdf, PDF p. 20

The completed explanation assumes no voluntary withdrawals and tops up to initial margin immediately after a below-maintenance settlement. The “deposit” column below follows that order, rather than assuming funds arrive before that day's price movement:

Day Beginning balance ($) Settlement ($/contract) Price change ($/contract) Daily gain/loss ($) Deposit after settlement ($) Ending balance ($)
0 0 82 — — 100 initial 100
1 100 84 +2 +40 0 140
2 140 78 −6 −120 80 100
3 100 81 +3 +60 0 160
4 160 79 −2 −40 0 120

Day 2 has an unadjusted balance of \(140-120=20\), below maintenance 40. Restoring initial 100 requires 80. The ending balance 120 is not a profit of 20: deposits were 180, so the trading loss is 60, matching \(20(79-82)=-60\). If the call instead restores maintenance, the day-2 deposit is 20 and later balances are 40, 100 and 60, still leaving the same −60 trading result relative to total deposits of 120. 02_seminar.pdf, PDF p. 20 L10(EssentialsOfFuturesTrading).pptx, slide 5–6

Self-assessment criteria and tutor checks

Unscorable means the response/conditions cannot be interpreted reliably; ask the existing prompt once for clarification, without adding a new assessment. Given a long/short, quote units, exposure, initial/maintenance balances and withdrawal rule, derive the strict margin-call price inequality, test equality and derive a withdrawal price condition for retaining initial or maintenance. Use a single uninterrupted price move before deposits/withdrawals; no tick grid is imposed unless stated.

sections.html: Motivation: What price first creates a cash call, and what price supports an intended withdrawal? Let \(X=Nq\) total exposure. Long balance \(A=I+X(F-F_0)\); short \(A=I+X(F_0-F)\). Use \(F\) in dollars if \(X\) is physical units. A call needs \(A<M\); equality is not a breach. To withdraw \(W\) while retaining \(K\), require \(A-W\ge K\), hence \(A\ge K+W\). \(K\) is a policy input; choosing initial versus maintenance changes this condition.
sections.title: Motivation, intuition, and definitions

sections.html:
1. Put the quote in consistent units and write the signed balance before any intervening cash adjustment.
  2. Substitute the strict-below criterion: long \(F<F_0-\frac{I-M}{X}\); short \(F>F_0+\frac{I-M}{X}\). Derive rather than memorize the adverse direction.
  3. At equality the loss exactly consumes the \(I-M\) cushion, so \(A=M\) and there is no call under this model. If a contract tick grid were supplied, the first allowed price strictly beyond threshold would matter; no grid is invented.
  4. Withdrawal needs \(A\ge K+W\). Long requires \(F\ge F_0+\frac{K+W-I}{X}\); short \(F\le F_0-\frac{K+W-I}{X}\). A withdrawal can be possible immediately if initial cash already exceeds \(K\)+\(W\).
  5. A target for a call and \(K\) for withdrawal are distinct rules. Source exercises do not set one universal withdrawal policy, so report conditional results and the exact assumptions.

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Problem 2: a short wheat contract; fingerprint b10a0ed1ddfde242583a447a4246738dc8f31af4dca1c5f77970596782335d04. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Problem 2: a short wheat contract

The company shorts 5,000 bushels at 250 cents per bushel, with $3,000 initial and $2,000 maintenance margin. Convert the quoted price to dollars: \(F_0=2.50\) dollars per bushel. A price increase harms the short. Before other deposits or withdrawals its balance at a new settlement price \(F\) is

\[A=3000+5000(2.50-F).\]

A call occurs when \(A<2000\), so

\[5000(F-2.50)>1000\quad\Longrightarrow\quad F>2.70.\]

Thus an increase of more than 20 cents per bushel, beyond 270 cents, breaches maintenance. Exactly 270 cents leaves $2,000, at the threshold under the stated strict-below rule. 02_seminar.pdf, PDF p. 18 L10(EssentialsOfFuturesTrading).pptx, slide 5–6

For a $1,500 withdrawal while retaining the initial $3,000, the account must first reach $4,500. The short needs a gain of $1,500, which requires a fall of \(1500/5000=0.30\) dollars per bushel. \(F\) must be 220 cents or lower. If only maintenance must remain after withdrawal, \(A\ge3500\) suffices, so \(F\) must be 240 cents or lower. The question does not specify which withdrawal rule applies; both conditional results are retained. 02_seminar.pdf, PDF p. 18 L10(EssentialsOfFuturesTrading).pptx, slide 5 02_seminar.pdf, PDF p. 13

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Problem 6: two orange-juice contracts; fingerprint b10a0ed1ddfde242583a447a4246738dc8f31af4dca1c5f77970596782335d04. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Problem 6: two orange-juice contracts

Two long contracts each cover 15,000 pounds, so total exposure is 30,000 pounds. Opening price is 160 cents ($1.60) per pound. Total initial margin is $12,000 and total maintenance is $9,000. A price fall creates a loss of \(300\) for each one-cent fall because \(30000\times0.01=300\). Before top-ups,

\[A=12000+30000(F-1.60),\]

with \(F\) in dollars per pound. Maintenance is breached when

\[30000(1.60-F)>3000\quad\Longrightarrow\quad F<1.50.\]

The call therefore follows a fall of more than 10 cents per pound, below 150 cents. Exactly 150 cents leaves the account at maintenance under the strict-below convention. 02_seminar.pdf, PDF p. 22 L10(EssentialsOfFuturesTrading).pptx, slide 5–6

To withdraw $2,000 while retaining total initial margin, the account must gain $2,000. This requires a price rise of

\[\frac{2000}{30000}=0.066\overline6\ \text{dollars per pound} =6.\overline6\ \text{cents per pound}.\]

Thus \(F\) must be at least \(1.666\overline6\) (\(166.\overline6\) cents), subject to the contract's allowed ticks, which the question does not specify. If retaining only maintenance is allowed, the original $12,000 already exceeds $9,000 by $3,000, so a $2,000 withdrawal is possible immediately. More generally the condition is \(A\ge11000\), or \(F\ge1.566\overline6\). The two results reflect different retained-balance rules rather than different futures gains. 02_seminar.pdf, PDF p. 22 L10(EssentialsOfFuturesTrading).pptx, slide 5 02_seminar.pdf, PDF p. 13

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage From daily result to an account balance; fingerprint c92b574f4c33c97bdbefad673c63cc8029a344a79d7b1da69ed2bba44076e313. Heading depth alone is adapted.

From daily result to an account balance

Let \(A_{t-1}\) be the previous ending account balance. Before any top-up or withdrawal, the new balance is

\[A_t^- = A_{t-1}+G_t.\]

If a call restores a target \(R\), the deposit is \(C_t=R-A_t^-\) when \(A_t^-<M\); otherwise there is no call. With a withdrawal \(W_t\), the ending balance becomes

\[A_t=A_t^-+C_t-W_t.\]

These equations are an explicit accounting synthesis of the source descriptions. A deposit increases the balance but does not create trading profit; a withdrawal decreases the balance but does not create trading loss. If a trader fails to meet a call, the exchange/clearing house can close the position through a reverse trade at that trader's cost. L10(EssentialsOfFuturesTrading).pptx, slide 5–6 FI01(Futures Contracts).doc, Ch. I, LibreOffice-rendered p. 4 02_seminar.pdf, PDF p. 12–13

The handout's five-day example

The complete source table has an opening price of 1,000 and both initial and maintenance margin equal to 200. Closing prices are 1,100, 1,200, 1,050, 950 and 900. The source uses a one-unit price-to-money normalization. FI01(Futures Contracts).doc, Ch. I, LibreOffice-rendered p. 9

The long receives 100 on each of the first two days, then loses 150, 100 and 50. Its cumulative gain/loss is therefore 100, 200, 50, −50 and −100. On day 4 the balance falls from 250 to 150 and a deposit of 50 restores it to 200. On day 5 the balance again needs 50. The long ends with 200 in the account after depositing 100 beyond its initial 200, but its trading result is −100. The account balance is not its profit. FI01(Futures Contracts).doc, Ch. I, LibreOffice-rendered p. 9

The short loses 100 on each of the first two days and posts 100 each time to restore 200. It then gains 150, 100 and 50, ending with 500. Total deposits were 400, so the account's net surplus over deposits is 100, equal to its trading gain. This compares the two positions' opposite cash transfers and illustrates why small initial deposits can require substantial later funding. FI01(Futures Contracts).doc, Ch. I, LibreOffice-rendered p. 9

sections.html: Motivation: Can the day's gains cover new margin even if the trader needs cash earlier? Old contracts settle from yesterday's settlement; new contracts settle from their entry price. Let \(n_{\mathrm{old}}\),\(n_{\mathrm{new}}\) counts, \(F_{\mathrm{old}}\) previous settlement, \(F_{\mathrm{entry}}\) new entry, \(F_{\mathrm{end}}\) today. \(G_{\mathrm{old}}=n_{\mathrm{old}}(F_{\mathrm{end}}-F_{\mathrm{old}})\); \(G_{\mathrm{new}}=n_{\mathrm{new}}(F_{\mathrm{end}}-F_{\mathrm{entry}})\). Initial margin \(m\) per contract implies beginning \(A=n_{\mathrm{old}}m\), new requirement \((n_{\mathrm{old}}+n_{\mathrm{new}})m\), increment \(n_{\mathrm{new}}m\). These equations use dollar-per-contract prices; other quote units need \(q\).
sections.title: Motivation, intuition, and definitions

sections.html:
1. Separate cohorts because the new contracts did not experience the entire prior-to-current price movement.
  2. Compute signed \(G\) for each, then sum \(G_{\mathrm{total}}\); one cohort may lose even when net gains.
  3. Compute incremental new margin \(n_{\mathrm{new}}m\) independently of \(\mathrm{P/L}\). This obligation exists even if settlement later funds it.
  4. Under end-of-day netting, available \(A_{\mathrm{beforefunding}}=n_{\mathrm{old}}m+G_{\mathrm{total}}\). Additional net \(\text{cash}=\max(0,\text{new requirement}-\text{available})\); \(\text{surplus}=\max(0,\text{available}-\text{requirement})\). Surplus is not total \(\mathrm{P/L}\).
  5. If incremental margin must be posted at entry before settlement, \(n_{\mathrm{new}}m\) temporary funding is needed under the assumed exact old balance. The resulting later surplus includes that deposit; do not count it as trade profit.
  6. With unspecified intraday sequence, present conditional net versus entry funding rather than one universal amount. This is account arithmetic, not a general broker policy.

Problem 5: clearing a larger long position

The member begins with 85 long contracts settled at $42,500 and initial margin $2,000 per contract. It adds 15 long contracts at $43,750. All contracts end the new day at $43,000. Existing contracts gain

\[85(43000-42500)=\$42,500,\]

while new contracts lose

\[15(43000-43750)=-\$11,250.\]

Net daily settlement is +$31,250. The 15 new positions require \(15\times2000=\$30,000\) additional initial margin. If the initial account holds exactly \(85\times2000=\$170,000\), the new requirement for 100 contracts is \(200,000\), while after settlement the account has $201,250. On an end-of-day net basis, no additional net cash is needed; $1,250 exceeds the new initial requirement. 02_seminar.pdf, PDF p. 21 02_seminar.pdf, PDF p. 11–13 L10(EssentialsOfFuturesTrading).pptx, slide 6

The required incremental initial margin is still $30,000. If it must be posted when the new positions are entered, before the day's $31,250 credit is available, it requires $30,000 of temporary funding. The PDF asks for total including initial margin but does not specify intraday sequencing, beginning excess balance or withdrawal rules. The answer therefore distinguishes the new margin obligation from net end-of-day funding rather than assuming their timing is identical. 02_seminar.pdf, PDF p. 21

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Daily profit and loss, with units; fingerprint c92b574f4c33c97bdbefad673c63cc8029a344a79d7b1da69ed2bba44076e313. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Daily profit and loss, with units

Let \(F_0\) be the opening futures price, \(F_t\) the settlement price at the end of day t, \(N\) the number of contracts and \(q\) the multiplier converting one quoted price unit into money per contract. With a constant position size and multiplier,

\[G_t^{\mathrm{long}}=Nq(F_t-F_{t-1}),\qquad G_t^{\mathrm{short}}=Nq(F_{t-1}-F_t)=-G_t^{\mathrm{long}}.\]

A price rise credits the long and debits the short; a fall reverses these transfers. The lecture writes the price difference for a normalized unit; \(Nq\) restores the contract units used by the seminar's tick examples. For a commodity quoted in dollars per pound, \(q\) is pounds per contract. For a contract quoted directly in dollars per contract, \(q=1\). L10(EssentialsOfFuturesTrading).pptx, slide 6 FI01(Futures Contracts).doc, Ch. I, LibreOffice-rendered p. 4–5 02_seminar.pdf, PDF p. 5, 12

Adding the daily transfers cancels every intermediate price:

\[\sum_{t=1}^{k}G_t^{\mathrm{long}} =Nq\big[(F_1-F_0)+(F_2-F_1)+\cdots +(F_k-F_{k-1})\big] =Nq(F_k-F_0).\]

The short obtains the opposite amount. This telescoping sum explains why the total trading result equals the closing minus opening price, even though it is paid in installments. The account can require cash along the way even when the final cumulative result is favorable. The source's reasoning ignores interest earned or paid on the timing of settlement cash flows. L10(EssentialsOfFuturesTrading).pptx, slide 6 FI01(Futures Contracts).doc, Ch. I, LibreOffice-rendered p. 7

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage The three margin concepts; fingerprint c92b574f4c33c97bdbefad673c63cc8029a344a79d7b1da69ed2bba44076e313. Heading depth alone is adapted.

The three margin concepts

Initial margin, \(I\), is the required deposit when opening a position. Both the long and short must post it. The lecture says it is the trader's money in the margin account, not the price paid for the underlying asset. Because it is only a fraction of the underlying contract value, it creates leverage: a given movement in the full contract's price can be large relative to this initial deposit. The seminar gives 5–15% as a usual illustrative range rather than a universal required rate. L10(EssentialsOfFuturesTrading).pptx, slide 5 FI01(Futures Contracts).doc, Ch. I, LibreOffice-rendered p. 4 02_seminar.pdf, PDF p. 11

Maintenance margin, \(M\), is the minimum allowed account balance. Daily losses may reduce the balance below \(M\). A margin call is then a notice to restore the balance to the specified target. The lecture allows a target of maintenance or initial margin; the handout describes restoring maintenance; the seminar's formula uses initial margin. The target must therefore be stated when doing calculations. L10(EssentialsOfFuturesTrading).pptx, slide 5 FI01(Futures Contracts).doc, Ch. I, LibreOffice-rendered p. 4 02_seminar.pdf, PDF p. 13

The lecture and handout call the extra deposited funds variation margin. The seminar also uses that phrase for the daily transfer of settlement gains/losses and writes “\(\text{Variation Margin}=\text{Initial Margin}-\text{Margin balance}\).” That expression describes a top-up to initial margin when the balance is deficient; it is not a formula saying every daily settlement payment equals \(I\) minus the balance. These meanings share the aim of limiting unpaid losses, but use different cash-account conventions. Below, “daily gain/loss” means the price-based transfer and “top-up” means the additional deposit after a call. L10(EssentialsOfFuturesTrading).pptx, slide 5–6 FI01(Futures Contracts).doc, Ch. I, LibreOffice-rendered p. 4 02_seminar.pdf, PDF p. 12–13

The seminar describes maintenance both as a minimum balance and as a payment made after adverse movement. The minimum is the threshold; the required payment is the amount needed to restore the chosen target. Keeping these quantities separate prevents confusing a $2,000 threshold with a $2,000 deposit in every case. 02_seminar.pdf, PDF p. 13

sections.title: Prerequisites and checks

sections.html: Motivation: A spot–futures gap and a two-maturity gap answer different questions. \(S_t\) is contemporaneous spot; \(F_t^{X}\) futures for earlier \(X\), \(F_t^{Y}\) for later \(Y\). Course basis \(B^{X}=S-F^{X}\); calendar spread \(D^{(X,Y)}=F^{X}-F^{Y}\). Contango \(F^{X}>S\) gives negative \(B\); backwardation \(F^{X}<S\) gives positive \(B\). Lecture normal contango \(F^{Y}>F^{X}>S\); normal backwardation \(F^{Y}<F^{X}<S\). Opposite sign conventions exist; name one explicitly. Week \(1\) names expectations, carrying/opportunity costs and expected payments as drivers, without a pricing derivation.
sections.title: Motivation, intuition, and definitions

sections.html:
1. Keep prices contemporaneous; compare spot against one maturity for \(B\) and futures against futures for D. Do not call D a basis.
  2. Substitute the declared signs. A negative \(B\) says futures above spot; a negative D says later above earlier. Labels follow those comparisons, not a forecast of rising spot.
  3. At delivery if \(F>S\), buy eligible asset spot for \(S\) and deliver using a short futures for \(F\), gross difference \(F-S\). If \(S>F\), obtain via long futures for \(F\) and sell spot for \(S\), gross \(S-F\). A borrowing-based spot short sale requires asset borrowing and return; short futures itself is a contractual sale.
  4. These executable positive differences drive theoretical \(F_T=S_T\)/\(B_T=0\) only under eligibility/matching delivery, feasible purchase/sale/borrowing and ignored costs. Nonzero costs or unavailable trades break the simple comparison; do not assert a free guaranteed trade in all markets.
  5. EDSP is contract-defined final settlement reference. Sources describe a closing procedure/selected-spot average but do not supply one universal computation. Convergence concerns each contract's own delivery endpoint; neither spot nor futures must move smoothly or monotonically. The source convergence asset illustrates curved paths.
sections.title: Explanation steps

sections.html:
Reading context

Deliver these complete reused passages before the worked example; the earlier concise teaching prompts are checkpoints, not substitutes. Necessary prerequisite lessons remain the routes specified above. Course-organization details in O001 are supporting context, not additional scoring components.

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Basis and calendar spread are different comparisons; fingerprint b3e4487925e9bd1ca9c2c341990863be4d2ff9f9a1e8e2211e1742e1bc4e5956. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Basis and calendar spread are different comparisons

For a delivery month \(X\), let \(S_t\) be the spot price at time t and \(F_t^X\) the futures price at that time for delivery in \(X\). This course uses

\[B_t^X=S_t-F_t^X.\]

The basis compares spot with one futures maturity. Contango means \(F_t^X>S_t\), so the basis is negative; backwardation means \(F_t^X<S_t\), so it is positive. Some markets use the opposite definition, \(F-S\); always state the convention before assigning signs. The seminar sometimes spells this quantity “Base,” but the lecture and handout use “basis.” L10(EssentialsOfFuturesTrading).pptx, slide 8 FI01(Futures Contracts).doc, Ch. I, LibreOffice-rendered p. 6 02_seminar.pdf, PDF p. 10

A calendar spread compares two futures prices. If \(X\) is the earlier delivery month and Y the later one, the lecture defines

\[D_t^{X,Y}=F_t^X-F_t^Y.\]

It also notes the opposite sign convention. The lecture's normal contango ordering is \(F_t^Y>F_t^X>S_t\), while its normal backwardation ordering is \(F_t^Y<F_t^X<S_t\). These are the meanings of those labels in the supplied lecture; do not substitute a different definition of “normal” without stating it. L10(EssentialsOfFuturesTrading).pptx, slide 8 FI01(Futures Contracts).doc, Ch. I, LibreOffice-rendered p. 7

The seminar lists market expectations, cost of carrying a position (including opportunity cost), and payments expected before delivery as reasons spot and futures prices can differ. Week 1 introduces these factors; the cost-of-carry pricing model in the later handout chapter is outside this ingestion scope. 02_seminar.pdf, PDF p. 10

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Why the prices converge at delivery; fingerprint b3e4487925e9bd1ca9c2c341990863be4d2ff9f9a1e8e2211e1742e1bc4e5956. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Why the prices converge at delivery

The source's no-arbitrage argument compares executable spot purchase/sale with delivery under the matching futures contract. If \(F>S\) at delivery, buy the asset spot for \(S\) and deliver it through a short futures position for \(F\). If \(S>F\), buy through a long futures position for \(F\) and sell the asset spot for \(S\). Either case produces a positive difference before trading, delivery or borrowing costs. The handout's examples use \(F=100\), \(S=80\) or \(F=80\), \(S=100\), producing a difference of \(20\) per unit. L10(EssentialsOfFuturesTrading).pptx, slide 9 FI01(Futures Contracts).doc, Ch. I, LibreOffice-rendered p. 6

The theoretical conclusion is \(F_T=S_T\), hence \(B_T=0\). It presumes the compared asset is eligible for the contract and the required purchases, sales and deliveries can occur on the relevant terms; otherwise the cash-flow comparison is not established. In the second case, the handout also describes selling a borrowed security spot, taking futures delivery and returning it. Short selling of the asset involves borrowing and later returning that asset; it differs operationally from merely opening a short futures position. FI01(Futures Contracts).doc, Ch. I, LibreOffice-rendered p. 6–7

The Exchange Delivery Settlement Price, or EDSP, is the price used in final settlement. The handout calls it the closing price on the last trading day, determined by the clearing house through an exact procedure. The lecture gives an average of selected spot quotations as its introductory description and says its determination implements zero basis. These descriptions establish that final settlement follows a defined reference procedure; they do not supply a universal formula covering every contract type. FI01(Futures Contracts).doc, Ch. I, LibreOffice-rendered p. 6 L10(EssentialsOfFuturesTrading).pptx, slide 7, 9

The green line is spot and the red lines are futures for the earlier month \(X\) and later month Y. Each futures line meets spot at its own delivery date \(D^X\) or \(D^Y\). The curves need not be straight or monotonic: convergence concerns the endpoint, not a prediction that either price moves smoothly toward it. L10(EssentialsOfFuturesTrading).pptx, slide 9

sections.html: Motivation: A losing futures leg can be part of a successful price hedge. \(X=Nq\) matched units; \(F_0\) opening, \(F_t\) closing, \(S_t\) spot at hedge transaction date; \(B=S_t-F_t\). A buyer opens long because a rise in later purchase cost should be offset by a futures gain. A seller opens short because a fall in sale receipt should be offset by a gain. Define \(E\) positive expenditure, \(\mathrm{CF}\) buyer signed cash flow with outflows negative, and \(R\) seller positive net receipt.
sections.title: Motivation, intuition, and definitions

sections.html:
1. Buyer: futures gain \(X(F_t-F_0)\); spot purchase costs \(X S_t\). \(E=X S_t-X(F_t-F_0)=X[F_0+(S_t-F_t)]=X(F_0+B)\). \(\mathrm{CF}=-E\).
  2. Seller: spot revenue \(X S_t\) plus short gain \(X(F_0-F_t)\). \(R=X S_t+X(F_0-F_t)=X(F_0+B)\). The same expression has a different economic label; do not swap buyer expenditure and seller inflow signs.
  3. At matching maturity conditional convergence \(B_T=0\) gives \(E=R=X F_0\) and \(\mathrm{CF}=-X F_0\). Futures loss on a falling market is offset by cheaper purchase; futures loss on rising market by higher sale price for seller.
  4. Before maturity the closing basis is unknown at inception. The early hedge still operates but leaves buyer expenditure \(E=XF_0+XB_t\) or seller receipt \(R=XF_0+XB_t\), rather than a guaranteed opening-price lock. This is basis risk, not the same as absolute spot movement.
  5. The notes flag the source verbal early-hedge sign error: \(-F_0+(F_t-S_t)=-F_0-B\), buyer signed flow. Positive expenditure is \(F_0+B\). Never reuse the mistaken label.
  6. Zero-basis effective-price accounting does not remove interim calls. Daily settlement requires funding and the source ignores its interest; a final hedge outcome is not proof of no cash demand.

sections.html:
Reading context

Deliver these complete reused passages before the worked example; the earlier concise teaching prompts are checkpoints, not substitutes. Necessary prerequisite lessons remain the routes specified above. Course-organization details in O001 are supporting context, not additional scoring components.

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage A purchase hedge, derived step by step; fingerprint b3e4487925e9bd1ca9c2c341990863be4d2ff9f9a1e8e2211e1742e1bc4e5956. Heading depth alone is adapted.

A purchase hedge, derived step by step

Suppose a buyer needs \(Nq\) units of the same underlying asset at maturity \(T\) and opens \(N\) matching long futures contracts at \(F_0\). Ignore transaction costs and interest on interim margin flows, as in the source's cash-flow arithmetic. By maturity the cumulative futures gain is \(Nq(F_T-F_0)\). Buying the asset spot costs \(NqS_T\). Net positive expenditure is therefore

\[E_T=NqS_T-Nq(F_T-F_0) =Nq\big[F_0+(S_T-F_T)\big] =Nq(F_0+B_T).\]

If convergence gives \(B_T=0\), net expenditure equals \(NqF_0\). A rise in the spot purchase price is offset by a futures gain; a fall reduces the spot cost but creates a futures loss. The hedge fixes the effective opening price under these matching assumptions. L10(EssentialsOfFuturesTrading).pptx, slide 10 FI01(Futures Contracts).doc, Ch. I, LibreOffice-rendered p. 7

The lecture instead writes signed cash flow with outflows negative:

\[(F_T-F_0)-S_T=-F_0-B_T=-F_0.\]

This is the same accounting with the opposite sign for expenditure. Defining the sign first avoids interpreting the negative amount as a negative purchase price. L10(EssentialsOfFuturesTrading).pptx, slide 10 FI01(Futures Contracts).doc, Ch. I, LibreOffice-rendered p. 7

The handout's five-day example ends at a spot and futures price of 900, after opening at 1,000. The long has lost 100 on futures, so buying spot for 900 costs 1,000 after that loss. This illustrates the hedge even though the futures leg itself is unprofitable. FI01(Futures Contracts).doc, Ch. I, LibreOffice-rendered p. 9

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage A sale hedge and early termination; fingerprint b3e4487925e9bd1ca9c2c341990863be4d2ff9f9a1e8e2211e1742e1bc4e5956. Heading depth alone is adapted.

A sale hedge and early termination

A seller expecting to have the matching asset opens a short. Its futures gain is \(Nq(F_0-F_t)\), while its spot sale produces \(NqS_t\). The net receipt at time t is

\[R_t=NqS_t+Nq(F_0-F_t)=Nq(F_0+B_t).\]

The long buyer's positive expenditure at the same time is also \(Nq(F_0+B_t)\), while its signed cash flow is \(-Nq(F_0+B_t)\). At maturity the source's zero-basis condition fixes both purchase expenditure and sale revenue at the opening futures price. Before maturity, \(B_t\) is unknown when the hedge is opened. This is basis risk: the uncertainty about the future spot–futures difference remains after the broad price movement has been hedged. L10(EssentialsOfFuturesTrading).pptx, slide 10 FI01(Futures Contracts).doc, Ch. I, LibreOffice-rendered p. 7

The handout says hedging is “possible only” on delivery dates, but its following formula explicitly describes an early hedge with remaining basis. Its operational distinction is between the exact opening-price lock at zero basis and the imperfect early hedge exposed to basis risk. The early net-cost formula exists; it does not guarantee a predetermined cost. FI01(Futures Contracts).doc, Ch. I, LibreOffice-rendered p. 7 L10(EssentialsOfFuturesTrading).pptx, slide 10

The handout's final early-hedge line writes \(-F_0+(F_t-S_t)\) but labels it “futures price − basis”. With its own definition \(B_t=S_t-F_t\), the displayed expression is \(-F_0-B_t\): the long buyer's signed cash flow. Its positive expenditure is \(F_0+B_t\). The verbal label therefore has an apparent sign inconsistency; the distinction between signed cash flow and positive expenditure above preserves the algebra. FI01(Futures Contracts).doc, Ch. I, LibreOffice-rendered p. 6–7, final early-hedge line on p. 7

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage What to carry forward; fingerprint b3e4487925e9bd1ca9c2c341990863be4d2ff9f9a1e8e2211e1742e1bc4e5956. Heading depth alone is adapted.

What to carry forward

A futures trading gain is only one leg of a hedge. Combining it with the matching spot transaction gives the opening price plus the remaining basis. At zero basis the hedge fixes the price; at an earlier date it leaves basis risk. The result depends on matching quantity, asset and maturity and on the source's cash-flow assumptions. Margins and marking to market explains why funding obligations may still arise before the hedge reaches its final result. L10(EssentialsOfFuturesTrading).pptx, slide 5–6, 10

sections.title: Motivation, intuition, and definitions

sections.html:
1. Identify numerator as the price difference for a normalized unit, then multiply by stated \(X=Nq\) when using full-contract money.
  2. Use annual \(r\) as a decimal with remaining years, or another consistently matched time unit. Denominator \(1+r\Delta t\) is dimensionless; \(V\) has money units after multiplying \(X\).
  3. The assumed maturity cash difference equals today's representation times \(1+r\Delta t\); divide to move backward under simple-interest assumption. This reasoning depends on payment being deferred, not paid daily.
  4. Long/short values are opposite. At inception \(F_t=F_0\) gives \(0\); at maturity \(\Delta t=0\) and, under convergence, \(F_t=S_t\), \(V_{\mathrm{long}}=X(S_t-F_0)\), short opposite.
  5. An actual margin account also contains deposits, withdrawals and daily realized transfers. Its balance cannot be inferred from this formula alone. Nor does this illustration value interest on every realized daily transfer. Do not call a negative \(V\) negative margin or a loss cap.

The lecture's value convention

The lecture labels \(S_T-F_0\) for a normalized long and \(F_0-S_T\) for a short as value at expiration. Those expressions equal the cumulative payoff described in the handout. Before expiration it presents a deferred-payment illustration:

\[V_t^{\mathrm{long}}=\frac{F_t-F_0}{1+r(T-t)},\qquad V_t^{\mathrm{short}}=\frac{F_0-F_t}{1+r(T-t)}.\]

Here \(r\) is the simple interest rate and \(T-t\) the remaining time in matching units. The denominator discounts a cash difference assumed paid at \(T\) back to t. At inception \(F_t=F_0\), so the source's value is zero. L10(EssentialsOfFuturesTrading).pptx, slide 11

Keep this illustration distinct from the lecture's actual daily marking-to-market mechanism. Slide 6 realizes changes day by day; slide 11 describes a price difference as income at maturity. The selected sources do not reconcile the timing conventions or provide a valuation of interest on all daily settlement flows. The discounted expression should therefore be learned as slide 11's stated deferred-payment representation, without treating it as the margin-account balance or as a proved universal value of a daily-settled contract. sections.html: An index quote has no money scale until multiplied by the contract multiplier. A minimum tick is a permitted quote increment; tick value is multiplier times that increment. For fixed long \(N\), \(G=N\times\text{multiplier}\times(F_{\mathrm{end}}-F_{\mathrm{start}})\); reverse the sign for a short. Closing ends the position; holding instead substitutes EDSP as the final endpoint. Do not add the whole held payoff to a closed payoff. Margin return divides trading \(G\) by the stated initial collateral, whereas contract exposure follows the multiplier and index level. Simple annualisation multiplies that fraction by \(365/\text{elapsed days}\); it magnifies short-horizon leverage and is not a prediction. EDSP is fixed by the contract's observation/trim rule: in the finished note's hypothetical example a sample of observations is taken and extremes removed. The specified benchmark is distinct from an arbitrary quote. Real contract terms require verification outside this prepared illustration.
