Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Read the contract before calculating; fingerprint 9934681819e12121ce3bdcd2bf33e74747d3ecc2cf2232b8981de7f2236997ac. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Read the contract before calculating

A quotation alone has no monetary meaning until the unit of trading and minimum price increment are known. Let \(N\) be the number of contracts, \(\delta\) the tick size in quotation units and \(v\) the money value of one tick. The change from opening quotation \(F_0\) to closing quotation \(F_t\) is \((F_t-F_0)/\delta\) ticks. Thus, before fees and financing effects,

\[\Pi_{\mathrm{long}}=N\frac{F_t-F_0}{\delta}v, \qquad \Pi_{\mathrm{short}}=-\Pi_{\mathrm{long}}.\]

This is a unit conversion: quotation change divided by quotation units per tick, multiplied by currency per tick. The long benefits when the quotation rises. The short benefits when it falls. The lecture's index and currency calculations use the same rule, even though their quoted units and settlement currencies differ. L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 4 L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 6

Margins and marking to market explains why daily transfers telescope to the opening-to-closing difference. Initial margin is a deposit supporting the position, rather than the value of the underlying asset. The tutorial return convention is

\[R_{\mathrm{period}}=\frac{\Pi}{N M_0},\qquad R_{\mathrm{annual,simple}}=R_{\mathrm{period}}\frac{365}{d},\]

where \(M_0\) is initial margin per contract and \(d\) is the holding period in days. This convention explains the large quoted returns: the denominator is margin, not the contract's full exposure. The annual figure linearly rescales the particular trade; it does not establish a repeatable annual investment outcome. In calculations using this convention, subsequent margin calls, withdrawals, fees and financing are outside the displayed denominator. L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 4 L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 6

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage SIFT 500: index points become euros; fingerprint 9934681819e12121ce3bdcd2bf33e74747d3ecc2cf2232b8981de7f2236997ac. Heading depth alone is adapted.

SIFT 500: index points become euros

The tutorial Stock Index Futures Tutorial 500 (SIFT 500) uses an index composed of share prices of the 500 largest companies by market capitalization. Its multiplier is EUR 10 per index point. A quote of 5,433 therefore represents EUR 54,330 of contract value. One tick is half an index point, worth \(0.5\times10=\text{EUR }5\); two ticks are one point. Initial margin is EUR 1,000, about 1.8% of EUR 54,330 in the source's example. L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 3

Tutorial specifications and footnotes, including the multiplier and final settlement averaging rule. L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 3

Delivery months are March, June, September and December. The last trading day is the last business day of that month, at 10:30 a.m.; delivery is the next business day. The exchange delivery settlement price (EDSP) averages underlying-index observations every 15 seconds from 10:10 through 10:30 a.m., discarding the 12 highest and 12 lowest values. This procedure aims to smooth excessive fluctuations shortly before maturity. It defines a final settlement benchmark rather than simply using the final observed index value. L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 3

Closing after five days

The long buys 20 contracts at \(F_0=5825.0\) and sells 20 matching contracts five days later at \(F_5=5812.5\). The quotation falls by 12.5 index points, equal to \(-12.5/0.5=-25\) ticks. Therefore,

\[\Pi=20(-25)(5)=-\text{EUR }2{,}500.\]

The return on opening margin is \(-2500/(20\times1000)=-12.5\%\). Simple annual scaling gives \(-0.125\times365/5=-9.125\), approximately the source's displayed \(-912\%\). A scaled return below \(-100\%\) reflects the short holding period and the chosen margin denominator; the observed five-day loss itself remains EUR 2,500. L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 4

Holding until cash settlement

Delivering every constituent share in the index's weights would create extremely high transaction costs, so the tutorial index contract settles in cash. If the position remains open, the final marking-to-market transfer compares EDSP with the previous day's closing futures quotation. The source gives EDSP \(5810.0\) and an additional loss of \(20(-5)(5)=-\text{EUR }500\). Its arithmetic treats \(5812.5\) as that preceding settlement quotation. This is an alternative to the five-day closing trade, not an additional payment owed after that trade has already closed the position. With the same opening quotation, the total hold-to-settlement loss is \(20(5810-5825)10=-\text{EUR }3{,}000\) (derived from the source's quotations). L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 4

The source timeline displays the closing quotation and final EDSP. Use the closing-out path and the maturity path as alternatives. L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 4

sections.html: EUR is the quantity delivered and USD/EUR is its unit price. Thus both invoice and futures gain are in USD. Let \(X=N\times25000\) EUR. A matched physical purchase costs \(XF_T\) USD. The cumulative long gain is \(X(F_T-F_0)\); subtracting it from the invoice leaves \(XF_0\). Dividing by \(X\) gives the initial USD/EUR quote. This algebra uses the same delivered quantity and endpoint and excludes funding, fees and mismatch. It does not imply the account needs no interim collateral. Closing earlier instead creates \(X(F_{\mathrm{close}}-F_0)\) and ends the contract: the final delivery branch is an alternative. The change from opening quotation \(F_0\) to closing quotation \(F_t\) is \((F_t-F_0)/\delta\) ticks. Thus, before fees and financing effects,

\[\Pi_{\mathrm{long}}=N\frac{F_t-F_0}{\delta}v, \qquad \Pi_{\mathrm{short}}=-\Pi_{\mathrm{long}}.\]

This is a unit conversion: quotation change divided by quotation units per tick, multiplied by currency per tick. The long benefits when the quotation rises. The short benefits when it falls. The lecture's index and currency calculations use the same rule, even though their quoted units and settlement currencies differ. L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 4 L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 6

Margins and marking to market explains why daily transfers telescope to the opening-to-closing difference. Initial margin is a deposit supporting the position, rather than the value of the underlying asset. The tutorial return convention is

\[R_{\mathrm{period}}=\frac{\Pi}{N M_0},\qquad R_{\mathrm{annual,simple}}=R_{\mathrm{period}}\frac{365}{d},\]

where \(M_0\) is initial margin per contract and \(d\) is the holding period in days. This convention explains the large quoted returns: the denominator is margin, not the contract's full exposure. The annual figure linearly rescales the particular trade; it does not establish a repeatable annual investment outcome. In calculations using this convention, subsequent margin calls, withdrawals, fees and financing are outside the displayed denominator. L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 4 L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 6

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage ECFT: identify the traded and invoice currencies; fingerprint 9934681819e12121ce3bdcd2bf33e74747d3ecc2cf2232b8981de7f2236997ac. Heading depth alone is adapted.

ECFT: identify the traded and invoice currencies

The Euro Currency Futures Tutorial (ECFT) trades EUR 25,000 per contract against the US dollar. The euro is the underlying/traded/base currency. The dollar is the invoice/variable currency. A quotation of \(1.2311\ \mathrm{USD/EUR}\) means that one euro costs 1.2311 dollars. The long receives euros and pays dollars at delivery; the short delivers euros and receives the dollar amount. L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 5

One tick is USD 0.0001 per euro, which the source describes as one hundredth of a US cent per euro. Its monetary value is

\[25{,}000\ \mathrm{EUR}\times0.0001\ \mathrm{USD/EUR}=\text{USD }2.50.\]

The EUR units cancel. Initial margin is USD 1,000, about 3.5% of the contract value when the exchange rate is 1.1345 USD/EUR. Delivery months are the same four quarterly months. The last trading day is the third Wednesday of the delivery month at 10:30 a.m.; delivery is the next business day. EDSP averages the rates of 15 reference banks at 10:30 a.m., excluding the three highest and three lowest. L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 5

The currency specification keeps quotation units, tick size and margin currency distinct. L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 5

Closing after ten days

The long buys ten contracts at \(F_0=1.2311\) and closes at \(F_{10}=1.2383\). The rise is \(0.0072/0.0001=72\) ticks, giving

\[\Pi=10(72)(2.5)=\text{USD }1{,}800.\]

The margin return is \(1800/(10\times1000)=18\%\). Simple annual scaling yields \(0.18\times365/10=6.57=657\%\). The gain is in dollars even though the underlying contract size is in euros. L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 6

Physical delivery fixes the effective purchase rate

If the ten contracts remain open until delivery, the long receives EUR 250,000. At EDSP \(1.2401\), the invoice is \(250000\times1.2401=\text{USD }310{,}025\). The opening-to-delivery gain is \(10(2401-2311)(2.5)=\text{USD }2{,}250\). Combining the invoice and the futures gain gives

\[\frac{310{,}025-2{,}250}{250{,}000}=1.2311\ \mathrm{USD/EUR}=F_0.\]

The long pays the EDSP invoice but has already received offsetting futures gains. This is why the effective purchase price reproduces the opening futures rate in the source's matched delivery example. The ten-day USD 1,800 gain and the delivery USD 2,250 gain describe different exit times and must not be added together. The calculation leaves funding timing and transaction costs outside the illustration. L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 6

The source currency timeline and invoice calculation show the alternative closing and delivery paths. L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 6

sections.title: Prerequisites and checks

sections.html: A futures price \(F=100-i\) uses \(i\) as an annual percentage, not a decimal fraction. A one-point price change is a one-percentage-point rate move in the opposite direction. A \(0.01\) quote-point tick represents \(0.0001\) annual decimal, so principal \(L\) and accrual fraction \(\tau\) imply tick value \(L(0.0001)\tau\). A lender loses spot interest when rates fall; a long future then gains because \(F\) rises. For matching principal, undiscounted effective interest cash is \(L i_{\mathrm{spot}}\tau+G\), so \(i_{\mathrm{effective}}=i_{\mathrm{spot}}+G/(L\tau)\). A consistent quarter-year tick and matching accrual \(.25\) produce the initial implied rate. The notes identify a different \(91/365\) fraction and payment-timing inconsistency; do not silently mix them or equate this simple algebra to an exact hedge including all daily cash-flow discounting. A physically arranged rate lower than the benchmark requires the separate \(\text{difference}\times\text{principal}\times\text{specified accrual}\) compensation; the benchmark and received rate are distinct.
sections.title: Motivation and explanation

sections.html:
Reading context

Deliver these complete reused passages before the worked example; the earlier concise teaching prompts are checkpoints, not substitutes. Necessary prerequisite lessons remain the routes specified above. Course-organization details in O001 are supporting context, not additional scoring components.

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Short-term interest rate futures; fingerprint 60171e496c1089e75dcac3575612a0518e958cac6a80dbe02da9b438b622a003. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Short-term interest rate futures

Why can a long interest-rate futures position gain when an interest rate falls, and how can a future deposit earn an opening rate agreed earlier? The tutorial contract quotes 100 minus an annual interest rate expressed in percent. Its price therefore moves in the opposite direction from that rate. Its tick value converts a one-basis-point annual rate change into the interest on a three-month EUR 500,000 deposit. These are hypothetical specifications, rather than current exchange terms. L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 2 L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 7

Quotation, tick value and the deposit period

The Three-Month Euro Interest Rate Futures Tutorial (IRF3T) has EUR 500,000 principal. With \(i_{\%}\) the annual interest rate in percentage points,

\[F=100-i_{\%}.\]

Thus \(F=90.50\) corresponds to a 9.50% annual rate for a three-month deposit. A one-basis-point change is 0.01 percentage point, or 0.0001 as a decimal annual rate. The source fixes the tick value using a quarter-year accrual:

\[v=500{,}000(0.0001)\frac{3}{12}=\text{EUR }12.50.\]

A higher quotation corresponds to a lower implied rate. The long's positive futures gain can then offset the smaller interest earned on a future deposit. The source calls the long the buyer of a certificate of deposit (CD), hence the lender, and the short the CD seller/borrower. For physical delivery, the long places EUR 500,000 in a three-month deposit at an eligible bank arranged by the short. L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 7

The complete specification includes the borrower/lender labels and the quarter-year tick derivation. L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 7

Initial margin is EUR 500, 0.1% of principal. Delivery months are March, June, September and December. The last trading day is the third Wednesday of the delivery month at 11:00 a.m.; delivery follows on the next business day. The source's specification describes EDSP as the three-month spot rate: the exchange samples 16 banks, removes the three highest and three lowest rates, and averages the remaining ten. The worked settlement example instead writes EDSP as a futures quotation, \(91.25=100-8.75\), so the underlying spot deposit rate is 8.75%. Keep rate units and quoted-price units distinct despite this source-label difference. L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 7 L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 8

Closing the futures before the deposit begins

The long buys one contract at \(F_0=90.50\) and closes two weeks later at \(F_{14}=90.55\). The five-tick rise represents a five-basis-point fall in the implied rate, from 9.50% to 9.45%. Its profit is

\[\Pi=(9055-9050)(12.5)=\text{EUR }62.50.\]

Using the source's opening-margin denominator, the 14-day return is \(62.5/500=12.5\%\). Simple annual scaling gives \(0.125\times365/14\approx3.26=326\%\). This closed position has no later delivery obligation. The result belongs to the margin trade, not a 12.5% interest return on EUR 500,000. L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 8

Cash settlement and the effective deposit rate

If the original position instead remains open to settlement, EDSP is shown as 91.25. Its 75-tick gain is

\[\Pi_T=(9125-9050)(12.5)=\text{EUR }937.50.\]

The accompanying spot deposit rate is 8.75%. A gain in euros can be expressed as an additional annual rate by dividing by principal and deposit-year fraction. For a principal \(L\) and deposit duration \(\tau\) years,

\[i_{\mathrm{effective}}=i_{\mathrm{spot}}+\frac{\Pi_T}{L\tau}.\]

This is the source's accounting interpretation: combine deposit interest with the settled futures gain. With the tick's own quarter-year convention, \(\tau=1/4\), the gain adds \(937.5/(500000/4)=0.0075\), or 0.75 percentage point. The effective annual rate is then \(8.75\%+0.75\%=9.50\%=100-F_0\). L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 7 L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 8

The slide's day-count and payment-timing qualification

Slide 8 converts the same EUR 937.50 using \(\tau=91/365\), rather than the \(3/12\) used for the tick value on slide 7. Its expression gives

\[0.0875+\frac{937.5}{500000}\frac{365}{91} =0.0950206\approx9.50206\%.\]

The slide reports this as 9.5%, so exact equality to the opening rate depends on keeping a consistent year fraction or accepting rounding. This difference is a source convention mismatch, not an extra market gain. L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 7 L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 8

The source also displays both \(500000\,r(91/365)=937.5\), giving \(r\approx0.00752\), and a discounted version

\[\frac{500000\,r(91/365)}{1+r(91/365)}=937.5,\]

giving \(r\approx0.00753\). The first treats the amount as interest over the period; the second treats it as a discounted amount. Slide 8 does not supply a full funding/timing convention reconciling these alternatives with daily marking to market. They should not be presented as one exact universal deposit-hedge identity. The reliable general result is the direction of the hedge and its unit conversion under an explicitly fixed accrual convention. L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 8

Physical delivery and compensation for a lower deposit rate

The source's physical example lets the short arrange a deposit at 8.70%, which is five basis points below the 8.75% EDSP spot rate. It compensates the long for that difference:

\[0.0005(500000)\frac{91}{365}=\text{EUR }62.33.\]

The five-basis-point compensation bridges the arranged rate to the benchmark. The opening-to-delivery futures gain bridges the benchmark to the opening futures rate. Both components are needed for the lecture's intended 9.5% deposit-rate interpretation, subject to the quarter-year versus \(91/365\) and payment-timing qualifications above. The diagram separates the futures trading period from the subsequent three-month deposit period, preventing those periods from being confused. L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 8

The source gives three alternative exit paths and uses two accrual/payment conventions in its effective-rate illustration. L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 8

What to carry forward

With this quotation, a long gains when the implied rate falls. Tick value depends on principal, the annual rate increment and the deposit duration. A deposit hedge combines the deposit's actual interest with futures gains and any delivery-rate compensation, using consistent units and day counts. Stock index and currency futures develops the common tick and margin-return calculation. The deposit application adds an interest-accrual period distinct from the futures holding period. L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 7 L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 8

A lender/depositor buys \(1\) at \(90.50\); it could close at \(90.55\) after \(14\) days or instead hold to price EDSP \(91.25\). Derive tick value and position direction; compute close \(\mathrm{P/L}\), margin return and simple \(365\)-day annualisation, held \(\mathrm{P/L}\), annual spot rate and effective deposit rate for matching total principal. For alternative physical placement at a rate \(0.05\) percentage point below the benchmark, calculate separate compensation using the same \(0.25\) fraction, add it to the actual interest and the held futures gain, and derive the final effective rate. Steps and interpretation: Tick in rate is \(0.01\text{ percentage point}=.0001\text{ annual decimal}\). \(\text{Tick money}=500000\times.0001\times.25=\mathrm{EUR}12.50\). Price rises when rate falls, so long hedges a lender against falling deposit rates; a borrower exposed to rising rates takes short. Close \(G=1\times 12.5\times (90.55-90.50)/.01=\mathrm{EUR}62.500000\); margin return \(12.5\%\), annualised \(325.893\%\). Held \(G=\mathrm{EUR}937.500000\); \(\text{spot rate}=(100-91.25)/100=0.087500\) annual decimal. sections.title: Prerequisites and checks

sections.html: Bond quotes are prices per \(100\) face. A \(100000\)-face contract therefore multiplies each quote point by \(1000\). Clean price omits accrued coupon; full price adds it. A conversion factor prices the deliverable at the contract reference yield, rather than its market yield: PV the remaining coupons and principal at the later coupon date, add the coupon due at that date and discount the combined cash value back to the earlier valuation date using the declared fraction, subtract reference accrued coupon, divide by \(100\). The finished-note example uses semiannual coupon \(4\) and periodic reference yield \(.035\); its later-date value \(P_{AN}=\sum_{j=1}^{22}\frac{4}{1.035^j}+\frac{100}{1.035^{22}}\). Earlier full value is \(P_F=(P_{AN}+4)/(1.035)^{\mathrm{fraction}}\), followed by the stated accrued-coupon subtraction and /\(100\). Its170/171 convention conflict prevents blindly copying a numerical factor. In prepared calculations \(\mathrm{CF}\) is declared consistently. Delivery cash per \(100\) is \(\text{futures clean price}\times\mathrm{CF}+\text{delivery accrued coupon}\). A short carry trade borrows, buys the cash bond, receives/reinvests coupons, delivers and repays. \(\text{Simplified daily carry}=\text{annual coupon}/365-\text{full purchase price}\times\text{funding rate}/365\). Positive constant carry rewards later delivery, negative earlier, only under the note's simplified conditions. \(\mathrm{CF}\) corrects reference characteristics, not actual funding economics; CTD needs eligible-basket comparison.
sections.title: Motivation and explanation

sections.html:
Reading context

Deliver these complete reused passages before the worked example; the earlier concise teaching prompts are checkpoints, not substitutes. Necessary prerequisite lessons remain the routes specified above. Course-organization details in O001 are supporting context, not additional scoring components.

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Bond futures, conversion factors and delivery; fingerprint a9656034a515703d258f470320f1ea171d1dcd964701cf8a1f19c755171cfec1. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Bond futures, conversion factors and delivery

How can one futures contract allow delivery of several real bonds when its underlying asset is a notional bond? Long-term bond futures specify a standardized reference instrument, then use a conversion factor to adjust the invoice for an eligible deliverable bond. The short chooses the bond and, in this tutorial, its delivery date within the month. Those options connect bond pricing to financing and coupon income. The lecture's hypothetical terms are recorded as supplied examples. L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 2 L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 9 L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 11 L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 13 L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 14

The notional contract and its monetary scale

The Long-term Treasury Bond Futures Tutorial refers to a notional 20-year Treasury bond with USD 100,000 face value and 7% yield to maturity. Its quotation \(QP\) is a clean price per USD 100 nominal value, excluding accrued coupon. Since \(100000/100=1000\),

\[CV=1000\,QP,\]

where \(CV\) is contract value in dollars. A tick is USD 0.01 in the quoted price, so it changes contract value by \(1000(0.01)=\text{USD }10\). Initial margin is USD 2,000, 2% of nominal contract value. Delivery months are March, June, September and December. The last trading day is two business days before the last business day of the delivery month. The short can deliver on any business day of the month. The source defines EDSP as the contract's futures price at 11:00 a.m. on the second business day before that last trading date. L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 9

The full hypothetical specification distinguishes the quotation per USD 100 from the USD 100,000 contract. L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 9

The source says the zero-basis-at-maturity rule is theoretically applicable to the CTD bond because the underlying reference bond is notional. This qualification links convergence to the eligible delivery choice rather than asserting that every bond's raw clean spot quotation equals the unadjusted futures quotation. The lecture does not derive a precise conversion-adjusted basis formula here. L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 9

A short closing trade

The short sells ten contracts at \(F_0=91.38\) and buys them back 45 days later at \(F_{45}=91.23\). The quotation fell by 15 ticks. A short benefits from that fall:

\[\Pi=10(15)(10)=\text{USD }1{,}500.\]

The initial-margin return is \(1500/(10\times2000)=7.5\%\). The source's simple annual scaling is \(0.075\times365/45=60.83\%\). This closes the obligation before the separate delivery illustration. Read the contract before calculating explains the common sign and margin-denominator rules. L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 10

Clean price, full price and coupon dates

A clean price excludes accrued coupon. A full price includes the compensation owed to the seller for coupon accrued since the previous coupon payment:

\[P_{\mathrm{full}}=P_{\mathrm{clean}}+AC.\]

All quantities must use the same face-value basis. A purchase of the source's eligible bond costs a full spot price, while the contract quotes clean. This distinction is necessary when comparing the initial cash outflow with the eventual delivery invoice. L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 9 L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 10 L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 14 L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 15

The eligible-bond example has USD 100 face value, an annual coupon of 8% paid semi-annually, hence USD 4 per coupon, and 12 years remaining from the previous coupon date. The timeline records a previous coupon on 18 November, purchase today on 1 April, the next coupon on 18 May, and the after-next coupon on 18 November. It displays a June delivery month, initial full spot price \(S_0=99.13\), initial clean futures quotation \(F_0=88.19\), and financing rate \(r=6\%\). These values belong to the delivery example, not the earlier \(91.38\to91.23\) closing trade. L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 10

The original delivery timeline keeps coupon dates, full spot price and clean futures quotation visible. Its displayed day counts are source assumptions; related inconsistencies are discussed below. L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 10

Conversion factor: price at the contract's reference yield

A bond's conversion factor \(CF\) is its clean price per one unit of face value when valued at the contract's 7% reference yield. It is dimensionless. The exchange calculates a factor for the first day of each delivery month and keeps that factor constant during the delivery cycle, using its specified rounding conventions. The source's adjusted clean delivery price is

\[P_{\mathrm{delivery,clean}}=CF\times FP,\]

where \(FP\) is the contract's futures quotation. Accrued coupon must then be added to obtain the full invoice price. A factor above one increases the clean invoice relative to \(FP\); a factor below one reduces it. In the source's valuation example, a coupon above the 7% reference yield gives \(CF>1\), and one below it gives \(CF<1\). This is a reference-yield adjustment, rather than a claim that different eligible bonds have identical current market prices or implied repo rates. L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 11 L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 14 L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 15

Follow the source's valuation steps

The coupon is USD 4 every half year and the reference half-year yield is \(0.07/2=0.035\). On the after-next coupon date, the source values 22 remaining coupon payments and the final principal:

\[P_{AN}=\sum_{t=1}^{22}\frac{4}{(1.035)^t}+\frac{100}{(1.035)^{22}} \approx107.584.\]

Here \(t\) counts half-year periods. Each payment is discounted to that coupon date. To obtain the full price at the beginning of June, the source adds the USD 4 coupon due at the later valuation date, then discounts back a fractional half-year. Its printed formula is

\[P_F=\frac{107.584+4}{(1.035)^{171/182.5}}=108.065\quad\text{(source's displayed equality)}.\]

It subtracts accrued coupon for 14 days to obtain a clean price:

\[P_C=108.065-\frac{14}{182.5}(4)=107.758,\]

and divides by 100 face value to give \(CF=1.07758\). The cash-flow reasoning is: discount future full value, remove accrued coupon, normalize by face value. L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 11

The conversion-factor example has a day-count error

The printed formula's 171 days disagree with the 170 days on the source timeline and with its numerical result. Evaluating the printed expression gives approximately \(108.044\) for \(P_F\), \(107.737\) for the clean price, and \(CF\approx1.077373\). Using 170/182.5 gives \(108.065\), \(107.758\) and \(1.07758\), matching the displayed results. These are agent recomputations from the original source formula and data. The note preserves both the printed formula and its discrepancy, rather than treating the stated factor as a verified consequence of 171 days. Use an explicitly supplied consistent factor for later calculations, or state a consistent day-count choice. L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 10 L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 11

Source conversion-factor definition, coupon timeline and printed calculations. The 171-day exponent and 170-day diagram are both visible. L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 11

The short's cost-of-carry transaction

The short borrows in the money market, uses the loan to pay the full bond purchase price, and acquires the bond. During the holding period, the bond produces coupon income while the loan produces a financing cost. At delivery, the short transfers the bond to the long, receives the invoice price, and repays the loan. The source calls

\[\mathrm{carry}=\mathrm{carry\ revenue}-\mathrm{carry\ expenditure}.\]

It uses accrued coupon as carry revenue and interest on the financed full purchase price as carry expenditure. This sign convention matters: positive carry means that continuing to hold the financed bond earns more than it costs. L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 12

The six labeled flows show borrowing, bond acquisition, delivery, payment and loan repayment. The diagram links cash financing to the physical delivery obligation. L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 12

Delivery timing under the source's carry rule

The source's rule chooses the last business day of the delivery month when daily carry is positive, and the first business day when it is negative. Its example computes, per USD 100 face value,

\[\mathrm{daily\ revenue}=\frac{0.08(100)}{365}=0.02192,\]

\[\mathrm{daily\ financing\ cost}=\frac{99.13(0.06)}{365}=0.01630,\]

so daily carry is approximately USD 0.00562. Continuing to hold adds positive carry, giving the source's choice of the last business day. With negative carry, waiting instead erodes the transaction's return. This is the lecture's simplified constant daily-carry rule. Its stronger sentence that in reality only the first or last business day is chosen is retained as a source assertion, not expanded into a universal market rule beyond the illustration. L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 13

What to carry forward

The contract quotation, full bond purchase price and full invoice price have different roles. Conversion factors adjust the clean delivery amount for a chosen bond, while accrued coupon completes the invoice. Carry links the bond's income to the financing cost and determines the source's delivery-date choice. Implied repo rate and cheapest to deliver develops the next question: which eligible bond gives the greatest return from purchase to delivery? sections.title: Prerequisites and checks

sections.html: A short-financed delivery resembles a loan: buy the full cash bond \(\mathrm{PP}\) at time \(0\) and receive full invoice \(\mathrm{IP}\) at delivery. With simple annual \(r\) and \(n\) days, the initial cash grows to \(PP(1+rn/365)\). If coupon \(C\) is received \(m\) days before delivery and reinvested at this same \(r\), receipts are \(IP+C(1+rm/365)\). Equating sides, collect \(r\) terms: \(r(PP n-Cm)/365=IP+C-PP\). A nonzero denominator therefore gives \(r=365(IP+C-PP)/(PP n-Cm)\). No coupon sets \(C=0\), yielding \(365(IP-PP)/(PP n)\). These are implied annual repo returns under the stated model, not a compounded project IRR. The finished-note source's printed \(3.57\%\) does not exactly match its given inputs: using \(43/180\) accrued coupon yields about \(3.61742\%\); the note exposes the mismatch. Prepared examples specify consistent full inputs, coupon dates and \(365\) convention. CTD maximises comparable eligible IRR; actual borrowing costs, fees and cash-flow timing decide realised profit. No actual basket in notes means no actual CTD can be named.
sections.title: Motivation and explanation

sections.html:
Reading context

Deliver these complete reused passages before the worked example; the earlier concise teaching prompts are checkpoints, not substitutes. Necessary prerequisite lessons remain the routes specified above. Course-organization details in O001 are supporting context, not additional scoring components.

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Implied repo rate and cheapest to deliver; fingerprint cc1472840d045ac50e647cb4be41302f7eeca6bf21ea19e86c7d6305b27d2153. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Implied repo rate and cheapest to deliver

Which bond should a short select when several bonds are eligible for delivery into the same futures contract? The lecture identifies the cheapest-to-deliver (CTD) bond as the eligible bond with the highest implied repo rate (IRR). IRR measures the annualized return implied by buying a bond at its full spot price and realizing the delivery invoice and any intervening coupon. Here IRR means implied repo rate throughout; it does not refer to a generic project internal rate of return. L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 14 L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 15

Bond futures, conversion factors and delivery explains the conversion-factor and accrued-coupon inputs. Selecting the lowest unadjusted clean market price would ignore the different delivery proceeds and coupon cash flows. The CTD comparison must consider the complete transaction on a consistent day-count and quotation basis. L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 14 L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 15

Why the return resembles a repo loan

The source compares an actual repo, in which cash is advanced against a bond and returned with interest, with a purchase-to-futures-delivery transaction. Buying the bond creates an initial cash outflow. Delivering the bond into the futures contract creates a later cash inflow. These flows can be described as an implied loan: the purchase amount is the advance and the delivery proceeds are its repayment. The bond may also pay a coupon before delivery, which the source assumes can be reinvested at the same implied rate until delivery. The short's actual money-market borrowing is a separate financing leg. L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 14

The initial outflow includes the clean market price and accrued coupon paid to the bond seller. The terminal inflow includes the conversion-adjusted clean futures price and accrued coupon paid by the receiver at delivery. If a coupon arrives before delivery, its reinvested amount also contributes to the terminal value. Thus IRR compares a complete stream of purchase and delivery cash flows, rather than comparing the futures quotation directly with the clean market price. L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 14 L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 15

Notation, units and assumptions

Use all prices on the same face-value basis, such as dollars per USD 100 face value. Define:

Symbol Meaning
\(PP\) Full purchasing price today
\(MP\) Clean market purchasing price today
\(IP\) Full invoice price at delivery
\(FP\) Contract's clean futures quotation
\(CF\) Deliverable bond's dimensionless conversion factor
\(C\) One periodic coupon payment
\(n_{T,DL}\) Days from today (\(T\)) to delivery (\(DL\))
\(n_{NC,DL}\) Days from the next coupon (\(NC\)) to delivery
\(AC_{PC,T}\) Coupon accrued from previous coupon (\(PC\)) to today
\(AC_{NC,DL}\) Coupon accrued from next coupon to delivery
\(AC_{PC,DL}\) Coupon accrued from previous coupon to delivery
\(AC_{T,DL}\) Coupon accrued from today to delivery when no coupon intervenes

The source formulas use simple annual rate accrual with day fractions \(n/365\). In the one-coupon case, they assume that coupon is reinvested at IRR. There are no fees or taxes in the displayed cash-flow equations. IRR is an implied transaction yield. Compare it with actual financing separately when discussing whether the financed transaction is profitable. L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 14 L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 15

One coupon before delivery

The purchase is \(PP=MP+AC_{PC,T}\). After the intervening coupon, accrued coupon restarts, so the delivery invoice is

\[IP=FP\,CF+AC_{NC,DL}.\]

The purchase amount accumulated to delivery must equal the invoice plus the coupon accumulated from its own payment date:

\[PP\left(1+IRR\frac{n_{T,DL}}{365}\right) =IP+C\left(1+IRR\frac{n_{NC,DL}}{365}\right).\]

The right-hand coupon interest covers fewer days because the coupon arrives after the bond purchase. Expanding and collecting the \(IRR\) terms gives

\[\frac{IRR}{365}\left(PP\,n_{T,DL}-C\,n_{NC,DL}\right)=IP+C-PP,\]

and therefore

\[\boxed{IRR=\frac{(IP+C-PP)365}{PP\,n_{T,DL}-C\,n_{NC,DL}}}.\]

The numerator is the undiscounted surplus, scaled to an annual rate. The denominator accounts for the amount and duration of invested cash, reduced by the coupon that arrives before delivery and can be reinvested. Both numerator and denominator use money times days, so the ratio is a dimensionless annual rate. The algebra requires a nonzero denominator. These intermediate steps are agent explanation of the source's displayed cash-flow identity, not extra empirical evidence. L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 15

Recompute the source's numerical example

The slide gives \(PP=99.13\), \(FP=88.19\), \(CF=1.07758\), coupon \(C=4\), \(n_{T,DL}=89\) and \(n_{NC,DL}=43\). The source's printed accrued coupon is \(4(43/180)\). Substituting its numbers literally gives

\[IRR=\frac{\left(88.19(1.07758)+4\frac{43}{180}+4-99.13\right)365} {99.13(89)-4(43)} \approx0.0361742=3.61742\%.\]

The slide reports 3.57%, which does not follow from those printed inputs. Using \(43/182.5\) instead gives about 3.56219%, close to its reported figure but still not identical. The preceding conversion-factor example also mixes a 170-day timeline with a 171-day exponent. These are source arithmetic/day-count inconsistencies. The generic cash-flow equation and its algebra are usable; the stated numerical example must not be taught as an exact verified answer. An exercise should give a consistent coupon day count and either a verified or explicitly assumed conversion factor. L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 11 L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 15

The diagram labels intervals of 46, 14 and 29 days, whereas the numerical formula uses 89 days from today to delivery and 43 days from the next coupon to delivery. Its printed calendar dates and displayed intervals should therefore be treated as the source's example conventions, rather than silently recalculated into a new calendar interpretation. L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 10 L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 15

The source includes both IRR cases, the complete notation and the numerical expression. Its 3.57% label and mixed day-count inputs remain visible for checking. L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 15

No coupon before delivery

Without an intervening coupon, the accumulated purchase amount equals the invoice:

\[PP\left(1+IRR\frac{n_{T,DL}}{365}\right)=IP,\]

where the invoice uses coupon accrued since the last payment,

\[IP=FP\,CF+AC_{PC,DL}.\]

Subtracting \(PP\) and dividing by the initial amount and time fraction gives

\[\boxed{IRR=\frac{(IP-PP)365}{PP\,n_{T,DL}}}.\]

The distinction from the one-coupon formula follows from the cash flows: there is no coupon to reinvest, so no \(C\) term enters the numerator or denominator. In the source's no-coupon setting, the short pays \(AC_{PC,T}\) at purchase but receives \(AC_{PC,DL}\) at delivery. The net accrued coupon is \(AC_{T,DL}\), provided the same coupon-accrual convention applies across the whole interval. L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 15

Compare eligible bonds and choose CTD

For each eligible bond, determine the full purchase price, its conversion factor, the delivery invoice, coupon cash flows and applicable dates. Calculate IRR using the case that matches those cash flows. The source defines CTD as the eligible bond with maximum IRR, and says exchanges calculate and publish IRRs. This does not mean the highest-coupon bond or the lowest quoted-price bond must be CTD. The invoice adjustment and acquisition cost matter jointly. The uploaded lecture supplies one worked bond, rather than a table of several candidates, so no actual CTD security is identified here. L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 14 L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 15

The source's carrying illustration finances at 6%. Using its literal numerical IRR inputs gives an implied yield around 3.62%, below that financing rate. This comparison is an agent inference from the supplied figures: a positive IRR alone does not establish a positive financed profit. CTD remains a comparison among the eligible delivery alternatives. L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 10 L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 14 L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 15

What to carry forward

Start with the full purchase outflow and finish with the full invoice plus any intervening coupon. The reinvestment assumption determines the one-coupon denominator. The CTD criterion is the greatest implied transaction yield among eligible bonds under comparable conventions. Reliable practice can use the source's formulas and explicit assumptions; exact reproduction of its inconsistent example requires clarification. L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 14 L11(ExamplesOfFinancialFutures).pptx, slide 15

sections.title: Motivation, intuition, and definitions

sections.html:
Origin: reused complete note introduction before the first subsection, Cost of carry and calendar spreads, fingerprint 7d0cb65d0bdf8c6f222c869632fef0242c46c9fb942547642920f337cf57f28d.

Cost of carry and calendar spreads

What determines a fair delivery price when an asset can be bought today, financed, and held until delivery? The lecture answers by constructing two ways to obtain the same asset at the same date. Comparing their cash flows removes the need to predict the future spot price. This is the core of Week 3 because currency, bond and index pricing are applications of the same replication logic. L12(CostOfCarryModel).pptx, physical slide 2–5

This source-grounded map follows physical slides 2–10; the present note develops slides 2–5, with the applications in the other Week 3 notes. L12(CostOfCarryModel).pptx, physical slide 2–10

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Foundations and conventions; fingerprint 7d0cb65d0bdf8c6f222c869632fef0242c46c9fb942547642920f337cf57f28d. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Foundations and conventions

\(S_0\) is today's spot price per unit of the underlying, \(F_0\) today's agreed delivery price per unit, and \(T\) the time to maturity in years. Annual decimal rates \(d\) and \(r\) represent respectively income/benefits and holding costs. The source lists coupons, dividends and convenience yield under \(d\), and interest, insurance, storage and deterioration under \(r\). In the linear model, income is \(dS_0T\), cost is \(rS_0T\), and net carry is \(S_0(d-r)T\). No particular calendar day-count basis is supplied. L12(CostOfCarryModel).pptx, physical slide 2–4

A long commits to buy and a short to sell. The foundational distinction is between paying for an asset now and agreeing a delivery price now: entering the idealized forward/futures position has zero opening value, whereas acquiring the asset costs \(S_0\). A financed spot position can nevertheless have zero net opening investment because the loan receipt pays for the purchase. No-arbitrage rules out a feasible zero-investment package with a sure positive payoff; if both the package and its reverse can be traded, its riskless payoff must be zero. These are model conditions, not a promise that any real investment earns a guaranteed return. L12(CostOfCarryModel).pptx, physical slide 2–4

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Borrow cash, buy spot and sell futures; fingerprint 7d0cb65d0bdf8c6f222c869632fef0242c46c9fb942547642920f337cf57f28d. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Borrow cash, buy spot and sell futures

At time zero borrow \(S_0\), pay it to buy one unit, and short one matching futures contract. Opening cash is \(+S_0-S_0+0=0\). At maturity the asset is delivered for \(F_0\), the loan principal \(S_0\) and its interest \(rS_0T\) are repaid, and the asset's income \(dS_0T\) is received. Under the source's deterministic simple-rate/timing assumptions,

\[\Pi_{\rm cash}=F_0+dS_0T-S_0-rS_0T.\]

Setting this to zero and collecting \(S_0\) terms gives

\[F_0=S_0+S_0(r-d)T=S_0[1+(r-d)T].\]

Financing raises the delivery price; income received while holding the asset lowers the net cost of replicating delivery. If quoted \(F_0\) exceeds this value, the package earns a sure positive modeled payoff: buy the asset cheaply through spot plus financing and sell the expensive delivery commitment. L12(CostOfCarryModel).pptx, physical slide 3

Source slide 3: opening loan/purchase cancel, and maturity inflows equal maturity outflows at the fair price. The asset's uncertain resale price does not enter because the asset is delivered under the agreed contract. L12(CostOfCarryModel).pptx, physical slide 3

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Borrow the asset, sell spot and buy futures; fingerprint 7d0cb65d0bdf8c6f222c869632fef0242c46c9fb942547642920f337cf57f28d. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Borrow the asset, sell spot and buy futures

For the reverse strategy, borrow the asset, sell it for \(S_0\), invest the proceeds and open a long matching futures position. Opening net cash is again zero. At maturity the deposit returns \(S_0+rS_0T\). Pay \(F_0\) to take delivery, return the asset to its owner and compensate the owner for income \(dS_0T\). Thus

\[\Pi_{\rm reverse}=S_0+rS_0T-F_0-dS_0T.\]

This is the negative of the first payoff. If \(F_0\) is too low, buy delivery cheaply and sell the asset now. When both strategies are feasible, neither sign can generate a riskless gain, forcing the equality above. Basis, carry, contango and backwardation

The course defines basis as spot minus futures, \(B_0=S_0-F_0\). Therefore

\[B_0=S_0(d-r)T.\]

If \(d>r\), net carry and basis are positive, so \(F_0<S_0\): the lecture calls this backwardation. If \(d<r\), carry and basis are negative, so \(F_0>S_0\): contango. If \(d=r\), \(F_0=S_0\). These price relations follow from the stated model and sign convention. A positive cost of carry \(r-d\) has the opposite sign to positive net carry \(d-r\); interchanging the terms reverses the conclusion. No forecast of future spot prices follows solely from these inequalities. L12(CostOfCarryModel).pptx, physical slide 3–4

What makes the replication valid

The lecture's linear rates, known income/costs, tradeable underlying, available short sales, matching delivery and locked funding underpin the derivation. A convenience benefit from physical ownership need not be a cash coupon transferable to a short seller. Thus listing convenience yield on slide 2 does not establish that every asset supports both exact arbitrages. External qualification: Damodaran's NYU “Futures Arbitrage,” sections “Storable Commodities” and “Stock Index Futures,” explains that funding differences, shorting costs and uncertain dividends weaken exact replication. These are reasons to inspect feasibility before applying the equation. Damodaran, consulted sections. L12(CostOfCarryModel).pptx, physical slide 2–5

The source aggregates all futures flows at delivery. Actual futures have daily variation margin, as explained in the Week 1 margin note. That cash timing, funding and reinvestment can matter; this note preserves the lecture's simplified replication rather than treating a forward-style cash-flow table as a complete margin-funding model. The simple formula also differs from compounded conventions: do not replace it silently by an exponential. L12(CostOfCarryModel).pptx, physical slide 3–5

sections.title: Try a carry calculation

sections.html:
Read the full checked source context

What determines a fair delivery price when an asset can be bought today, financed, and held until delivery? The lecture answers by constructing two ways to obtain the same asset at the same date. Comparing their cash flows removes the need to predict the future spot price. This is the core of Week 3 because currency, bond and index pricing are applications of the same replication logic. L12(CostOfCarryModel).pptx, physical slide 2–5

This source-grounded map follows physical slides 2–10; the present note develops slides 2–5, with the applications in the other Week 3 notes. L12(CostOfCarryModel).pptx, physical slide 2–10

Foundations and conventions

\(S_0\) is today's spot price per unit of the underlying, \(F_0\) today's agreed delivery price per unit, and \(T\) the time to maturity in years. Annual decimal rates \(d\) and \(r\) represent respectively income/benefits and holding costs. The source lists coupons, dividends and convenience yield under \(d\), and interest, insurance, storage and deterioration under \(r\). In the linear model, income is \(dS_0T\), cost is \(rS_0T\), and net carry is \(S_0(d-r)T\). No particular calendar day-count basis is supplied. L12(CostOfCarryModel).pptx, physical slide 2–4

A long commits to buy and a short to sell. The foundational distinction is between paying for an asset now and agreeing a delivery price now: entering the idealized forward/futures position has zero opening value, whereas acquiring the asset costs \(S_0\). A financed spot position can nevertheless have zero net opening investment because the loan receipt pays for the purchase. No-arbitrage rules out a feasible zero-investment package with a sure positive payoff; if both the package and its reverse can be traded, its riskless payoff must be zero. These are model conditions, not a promise that any real investment earns a guaranteed return. L12(CostOfCarryModel).pptx, physical slide 2–4

Borrow cash, buy spot and sell futures

At time zero borrow \(S_0\), pay it to buy one unit, and short one matching futures contract. Opening cash is \(+S_0-S_0+0=0\). At maturity the asset is delivered for \(F_0\), the loan principal \(S_0\) and its interest \(rS_0T\) are repaid, and the asset's income \(dS_0T\) is received. Under the source's deterministic simple-rate/timing assumptions,

\[\Pi_{\rm cash}=F_0+dS_0T-S_0-rS_0T.\]

Setting this to zero and collecting \(S_0\) terms gives

\[F_0=S_0+S_0(r-d)T=S_0[1+(r-d)T].\]

Financing raises the delivery price; income received while holding the asset lowers the net cost of replicating delivery. If quoted \(F_0\) exceeds this value, the package earns a sure positive modeled payoff: buy the asset cheaply through spot plus financing and sell the expensive delivery commitment. L12(CostOfCarryModel).pptx, physical slide 3

Source slide 3: opening loan/purchase cancel, and maturity inflows equal maturity outflows at the fair price. The asset's uncertain resale price does not enter because the asset is delivered under the agreed contract. L12(CostOfCarryModel).pptx, physical slide 3

Borrow the asset, sell spot and buy futures

For the reverse strategy, borrow the asset, sell it for \(S_0\), invest the proceeds and open a long matching futures position. Opening net cash is again zero. At maturity the deposit returns \(S_0+rS_0T\). Pay \(F_0\) to take delivery, return the asset to its owner and compensate the owner for income \(dS_0T\). Thus

\[\Pi_{\rm reverse}=S_0+rS_0T-F_0-dS_0T.\]

This is the negative of the first payoff. If \(F_0\) is too low, buy delivery cheaply and sell the asset now. When both strategies are feasible, neither sign can generate a riskless gain, forcing the equality above. In this strategy \(r\) is the modeled deposit return, whereas slide 3 uses it as financing cost; the common rate and reversible cash flows are substantive assumptions. Shorting restrictions or different borrowing/lending terms can replace one exact price by a range. L12(CostOfCarryModel).pptx, physical slide 4

Basis, carry, contango and backwardation

The course defines basis as spot minus futures, \(B_0=S_0-F_0\). Therefore

\[B_0=S_0(d-r)T.\]

If \(d>r\), net carry and basis are positive, so \(F_0<S_0\): the lecture calls this backwardation. If \(d<r\), carry and basis are negative, so \(F_0>S_0\): contango. If \(d=r\), \(F_0=S_0\). These price relations follow from the stated model and sign convention. A positive cost of carry \(r-d\) has the opposite sign to positive net carry \(d-r\); interchanging the terms reverses the conclusion. No forecast of future spot prices follows solely from these inequalities. L12(CostOfCarryModel).pptx, physical slide 3–4

Carry between two delivery dates

Let \(F_0^1,F_0^2\) be current prices for deliveries at \(T^1<T^2\), both measured in years, and put \(\Delta T=T^2-T^1\). Today go long the earlier contract, short the later one, and arrange a forward loan for the interval \([T^1,T^2]\). The source assigns zero initial cash to each agreement. At \(T^1\) draw \(F_0^1\) under the arranged loan and pay the earlier contract to acquire the asset. Hold it only for \(\Delta T\); the source measures income and financing cost relative to the amount \(F_0^1\) financed. At \(T^2\) deliver for \(F_0^2\) and repay the loan:

\[0=[F_0^2+dF_0^1\Delta T]-[F_0^1+rF_0^1\Delta T].\]

Moving the delivery-price terms to one side gives

\[F_0^1-F_0^2=F_0^1(d-r)(T^2-T^1),\qquad F_0^2=F_0^1[1+(r-d)\Delta T].\]

The earlier-minus-later spread equals carry over the intervening interval. Using \(T^2\) instead of \(T^2-T^1\) would charge for time before the asset was acquired. Using \(S_0\) rather than \(F_0^1\) would change the financing base in the source's construction. This is a separate interval model with funding terms locked today, not a license to combine inconsistent rates across maturities. L12(CostOfCarryModel).pptx, physical slide 5

What makes the replication valid

The lecture's linear rates, known income/costs, tradeable underlying, available short sales, matching delivery and locked funding underpin the derivation. A convenience benefit from physical ownership need not be a cash coupon transferable to a short seller. Thus listing convenience yield on slide 2 does not establish that every asset supports both exact arbitrages. External qualification: Damodaran's NYU “Futures Arbitrage,” sections “Storable Commodities” and “Stock Index Futures,” explains that funding differences, shorting costs and uncertain dividends weaken exact replication. These are reasons to inspect feasibility before applying the equation. Damodaran, consulted sections. L12(CostOfCarryModel).pptx, physical slide 2–5

The source aggregates all futures flows at delivery. Actual futures have daily variation margin, as explained in the Week 1 margin note. That cash timing, funding and reinvestment can matter; this note preserves the lecture's simplified replication rather than treating a forward-style cash-flow table as a complete margin-funding model. The simple formula also differs from compounded conventions: do not replace it silently by an exponential. L12(CostOfCarryModel).pptx, physical slide 3–5

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Carry between two delivery dates; fingerprint 7d0cb65d0bdf8c6f222c869632fef0242c46c9fb942547642920f337cf57f28d. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Carry between two delivery dates

Let \(F_0^1,F_0^2\) be current prices for deliveries at \(T^1<T^2\), both measured in years, and put \(\Delta T=T^2-T^1\). Today go long the earlier contract, short the later one, and arrange a forward loan for the interval \([T^1,T^2]\). The source assigns zero initial cash to each agreement. At \(T^1\) draw \(F_0^1\) under the arranged loan and pay the earlier contract to acquire the asset. Hold it only for \(\Delta T\); the source measures income and financing cost relative to the amount \(F_0^1\) financed. At \(T^2\) deliver for \(F_0^2\) and repay the loan:

\[0=[F_0^2+dF_0^1\Delta T]-[F_0^1+rF_0^1\Delta T].\]

Moving the delivery-price terms to one side gives

\[F_0^1-F_0^2=F_0^1(d-r)(T^2-T^1),\qquad F_0^2=F_0^1[1+(r-d)\Delta T].\]

The earlier-minus-later spread equals carry over the intervening interval. Using \(T^2\) instead of \(T^2-T^1\) would charge for time before the asset was acquired. Using \(S_0\) rather than \(F_0^1\) would change the financing base in the source's construction. This is a separate interval model with funding terms locked today, not a license to combine inconsistent rates across maturities. L12(CostOfCarryModel).pptx, physical slide 5

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage What makes the replication valid; fingerprint 7d0cb65d0bdf8c6f222c869632fef0242c46c9fb942547642920f337cf57f28d. Heading depth alone is adapted.

What makes the replication valid

The lecture's linear rates, known income/costs, tradeable underlying, available short sales, matching delivery and locked funding underpin the derivation. A convenience benefit from physical ownership need not be a cash coupon transferable to a short seller. Thus listing convenience yield on slide 2 does not establish that every asset supports both exact arbitrages. External qualification: Damodaran's NYU “Futures Arbitrage,” sections “Storable Commodities” and “Stock Index Futures,” explains that funding differences, shorting costs and uncertain dividends weaken exact replication. These are reasons to inspect feasibility before applying the equation. Damodaran, consulted sections. L12(CostOfCarryModel).pptx, physical slide 2–5

The source aggregates all futures flows at delivery. Actual futures have daily variation margin, as explained in the Week 1 margin note. That cash timing, funding and reinvestment can matter; this note preserves the lecture's simplified replication rather than treating a forward-style cash-flow table as a complete margin-funding model. The simple formula also differs from compounded conventions: do not replace it silently by an exponential. L12(CostOfCarryModel).pptx, physical slide 3–5

Currency parity and carry trade

How can interest rates determine a forward exchange rate, yet a currency carry trade still lose money? The distinction is whether the future conversion is contracted today or left exposed to the future spot rate. This note derives the course's covered relation before explaining its uncovered and peg-dependent examples. L12(CostOfCarryModel).pptx, physical slide 6–8

The map follows slides 6–8; the prerequisite is matching assets, dates and cash flows in the general carry model. L12(CostOfCarryModel).pptx, physical slide 6–8

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Covered interest parity with dollars per euro; fingerprint 9aaebd51a4ce2a4c8964bbf02d522f5ea81dbc1fbb36583d7990849bc3299c8d. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Covered interest parity with dollars per euro

On slide 6, \(S_0\) and \(F_0\) mean dollars per euro. Let \(r_\$,r_€\) be annual simple dollar/euro rates and \(\tau=T/12\) years when the slide's \(T\) is in months. Borrow one euro, sell it for \(S_0\) dollars and deposit those dollars. At maturity the deposit pays \(S_0(1+r_\$\tau)\) dollars. The euro debt is \(1+r_€\tau\) euros; arrange a forward purchase of that euro amount, equivalently a forward sale of the corresponding dollar deposit proceeds at parity. The locked dollar repayment cost is \(F_0(1+r_€\tau)\). Setting the zero-investment package's dollar payoff to zero gives

\[S_0(1+r_\$\tau)=F_0(1+r_€\tau),\qquad F_0=S_0\frac{1+r_\$\tau}{1+r_€\tau}.\]

The numerator/denominator follow the quotation: dollar investment grows at the dollar rate, but each euro owed costs \(F_0\) dollars. No uncertain future spot conversion remains in this covered package. L12(CostOfCarryModel).pptx, physical slide 6

Dividing by \(S_0\) and subtracting from one yields the slide's exact relation

\[\frac{S_0-F_0}{S_0}=\frac{(r_€-r_\$)\tau}{1+r_€\tau}\approx(r_€-r_\$)\tau.\]

The approximation ignores the denominator's deviation from one; it is not an exact annualized percentage. If \(r_€>r_\$\), \(F_0<S_0\): one euro buys fewer dollars forward, a euro forward discount/dollar premium. If \(r_€<r_\$\) the euro is at a premium. Reversing the currency quotation requires rederiving the ratio rather than keeping its sign mechanically. Rates, value dates and borrowing/lending availability must match. L12(CostOfCarryModel).pptx, physical slide 6

The source table shows principal and interest separately; the equations above group them into maturity balances. The slide's month-to-year conversion is essential even though other slides measure \(T\) directly in years. L12(CostOfCarryModel).pptx, physical slide 6

O016-W1, item_version 1, worked_example. Prompt: The spot quote is \(S_0=1.2\ \mathrm{USD/EUR}\). Annual simple rates are \(r_\$=0.06\) and \(r_€=0.02\); maturity is 6 months. Matching value dates, equal relevant borrowing/lending terms and covered forward trades are available. Borrow one euro and derive covered interest parity by matching every maturity currency amount. Compute fair \(F_0\), the exact normalized spot-minus-forward difference and its first-order approximation. Name which currency has a premium/discount under this quotation. For a quote \(1.23376238\ \mathrm{USD/EUR}\) above parity, construct the reverse covered package and compute its USD payoff per initial euro acquired. Explain why the covered conclusion is not an uncovered expected-spot forecast and why quotation/time units matter.

Complete solution and essential rubric: Use \(\tau=6/12=0.5\) years. Borrow EUR 1, sell for USD \(1.2\) and invest to \(S_0(1+r_\$\tau)=1.23600000\) USD. Euro debt is \(1+r_€\tau=1.01000000\) EUR; forward repayment costs \(F_0(1+r_€\tau)\) USD. Equalizing gives \(F_0=S_0(1+r_\$\tau)/(1+r_€\tau)=1.22376238\ \mathrm{USD/EUR}\). The exact \((S_0-F_0)/S_0=((r_€-r_\$)\tau)/(1+r_€\tau)=-0.01980198\), versus approximation \((r_€-r_\$)\tau=-0.02000000\); denominator is omitted only approximately. Euro forward premium/dollar discount because USD per EUR increases. For an overpriced euro forward, borrow USD \(1.2\), buy EUR 1, invest it to EUR \(1.01000000\) and sell that maturity amount forward. USD receipt minus USD debt is \(F_{\mathrm{quote}}(1+r_€\tau)-S_0(1+r_\$\tau)=0.01010000\). Contracting the entire conversion removes future-spot risk under the assumptions. Replacing the forward with an expectation leaves realized spot random; no UIP forecast is proved. Inverting quotation requires rederiving numerator/denominator and premium sign; using months as years misstates accrual. Matching dates and feasible rates are required. sections.title: Content provenance and generation boundaries

sections.html:
Read the full checked source context

How can interest rates determine a forward exchange rate, yet a currency carry trade still lose money? The distinction is whether the future conversion is contracted today or left exposed to the future spot rate. This note derives the course's covered relation before explaining its uncovered and peg-dependent examples. L12(CostOfCarryModel).pptx, physical slide 6–8

The map follows slides 6–8; the prerequisite is matching assets, dates and cash flows in the general carry model. L12(CostOfCarryModel).pptx, physical slide 6–8

Covered interest parity with dollars per euro

On slide 6, \(S_0\) and \(F_0\) mean dollars per euro. Let \(r_\$,r_€\) be annual simple dollar/euro rates and \(\tau=T/12\) years when the slide's \(T\) is in months. Borrow one euro, sell it for \(S_0\) dollars and deposit those dollars. At maturity the deposit pays \(S_0(1+r_\$\tau)\) dollars. The euro debt is \(1+r_€\tau\) euros; arrange a forward purchase of that euro amount, equivalently a forward sale of the corresponding dollar deposit proceeds at parity. The locked dollar repayment cost is \(F_0(1+r_€\tau)\). Setting the zero-investment package's dollar payoff to zero gives

\[S_0(1+r_\$\tau)=F_0(1+r_€\tau),\qquad F_0=S_0\frac{1+r_\$\tau}{1+r_€\tau}.\]

The numerator/denominator follow the quotation: dollar investment grows at the dollar rate, but each euro owed costs \(F_0\) dollars. No uncertain future spot conversion remains in this covered package. L12(CostOfCarryModel).pptx, physical slide 6

Dividing by \(S_0\) and subtracting from one yields the slide's exact relation

\[\frac{S_0-F_0}{S_0}=\frac{(r_€-r_\$)\tau}{1+r_€\tau}\approx(r_€-r_\$)\tau.\]

The approximation ignores the denominator's deviation from one; it is not an exact annualized percentage. If \(r_€>r_\$\), \(F_0<S_0\): one euro buys fewer dollars forward, a euro forward discount/dollar premium. If \(r_€<r_\$\) the euro is at a premium. Reversing the currency quotation requires rederiving the ratio rather than keeping its sign mechanically. Rates, value dates and borrowing/lending availability must match. L12(CostOfCarryModel).pptx, physical slide 6

The source table shows principal and interest separately; the equations above group them into maturity balances. The slide's month-to-year conversion is essential even though other slides measure \(T\) directly in years. L12(CostOfCarryModel).pptx, physical slide 6

Uncovered parity is a condition on expectations

Slide 7 replaces \(F_0\) by \(E_0[S_T]\) (the source writes \(E_T(S)\) for the anticipated maturity spot rate) in the dollar-per-euro relation:

\[\frac{S_0-E_0[S_T]}{S_0}=\frac{(r_€-r_\$)\tau}{1+r_€\tau}.\]

Without a forward contract the actual \(S_T\) remains unknown. This equation is an uncovered interest parity hypothesis, rather than an equality forced by a riskless trading package. A higher-yield currency must be expected to depreciate sufficiently under that condition to offset its interest advantage. Expectations are not realized cash flows; replacing a future random conversion with its expectation does not remove risk. L12(CostOfCarryModel).pptx, physical slide 7

External verification: Cavallo (2006), “Interest Rates, Carry Trades, and Exchange Rate Movements,” sections “Not profitable in theory, but profitable in practice” and “What is the carry trade?”, distinguishes the parity condition from exchange risk in the actual strategy. This supports the risk qualification; its empirical examples are not additional course assignments. FRBSF Economic Letter 2006-31.

The lecture's peg and non-deliverable-forward example

The source switches to Czechoslovak koruna per Deutsche Mark, \(S_{\rm CSK/DEM}\). With \(r_{\rm CSK}>r_{\rm DEM}\) the covered forward rate satisfies \(F_{\rm CSK/DEM}>S_{\rm CSK/DEM}\). If the future spot rate actually stays at the present peg, selling one DEM forward and buying it spot at maturity earns \(F-S_T=F-S_0>0\) koruna. That is the logic behind the lecture's bundled bank trade. The source explicitly mentions fluctuation bands and a peg to a currency basket as practical complications. L12(CostOfCarryModel).pptx, physical slide 7

Necessary qualification of the source: slide 7 calls the payoff “risk-free” after replacing future spot by its expectation. A peg or the belief \(E_0[S_T]=S_0\) alone does not guarantee \(S_T=S_0\). If the peg changes and \(S_T>F\), the short DEM forward loses. The source's positive result is conditional on an unchanged executable conversion rate and ignored costs/counterparty constraints. It cannot be generalized into riskless profit merely from a fixed-exchange-rate announcement. L12(CostOfCarryModel).pptx, physical slide 7

Supplementary definition: an NDF settles a contractual exchange-rate difference in cash, rather than delivering the underlying currency principal. It is not defined by an interest-differential profit or a peg. This distinguishes the source's particular strategy from the instrument's general definition. See McCauley, Shu and Ma (2014), “Non-deliverable forwards: 2013 and beyond,” opening definition paragraphs, BIS Quarterly Review: NDF definition. Contract-specific settlement currency and fixing must be checked; the course does not supply such terms for this historical example.

Yen-funded dollar carry trade

Slide 8 uses yet another quotation: \(S_0\) is yen per dollar, and the horizon is one year. Borrow one yen at \(r_¥\), convert it into \(1/S_0\) dollars and invest at \(r_\$\). At maturity the dollar balance is \((1+r_\$)/S_0\). Converting at realized \(S_T\) gives \(S_T(1+r_\$)/S_0\) yen. Repaying \(1+r_¥\) leaves

\[\Pi_T=\frac{S_T}{S_0}(1+r_\$)-(1+r_¥)\quad\text{yen per initial yen borrowed}.\]

Taking expectations gives the slide's expression with \(E_0[S_T]\). If the exchange rate stays unchanged, profit is \(r_\$-r_¥\). A higher dollar interest rate therefore creates a carry incentive, but yen appreciation means fewer yen per dollar, so \(S_T\) falls and repayment becomes harder. The strategy breaks even when

\[\frac{S_T}{S_0}=\frac{1+r_¥}{1+r_\$}.\]

Setting expected rather than realized profit to zero gives the corresponding uncovered parity condition. Negative expected exchange movement can offset a positive interest differential; an unexpected stronger movement can produce a loss. L12(CostOfCarryModel).pptx, physical slide 8

Agent-created illustration from that equation: at \(S_0=100\) yen/dollar, \(r_\$=5\%\), \(r_¥=1\%\), unchanged spot produces \(0.04\) yen per yen borrowed. Break-even is \(S_T=100(1.01/1.05)\approx96.19\). If \(S_T=90\), profit is \(0.9(1.05)-1.01=-0.065\) yen. This is arithmetic under the slide's one-year setup, not a supplied historical result or trading recommendation. L12(CostOfCarryModel).pptx, physical slide 8

sections.html:
O017-W1, item_version 1, worked_example. Prompt: Borrow one yen for one year at \(r_¥=0.01\), convert at \(S_0=100\ \mathrm{JPY/USD}\) and invest in dollars at \(r_\$=0.05\). No forward covers the dollar conversion. Derive realized yen profit per initial yen, calculate profit at unchanged spot, the break-even spot and profit at \(S_T=90\). Contrast a zero expected profit/UIP condition with a guaranteed realized payoff and explain the direction of funding-currency appreciation. Separately a historical-style peg example quotes koruna per DEM: spot peg \(20\), short DEM-forward delivery price \(21\), and possible terminal spot \(23\). Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Zero-coupon prices and dates; fingerprint d7ab9842da46a637253eee946ddc40c7fda3e5255580ef0b62c78c83b2ff16d4. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Zero-coupon prices and dates

A zero-coupon bond pays only face value \(M\) at maturity. Let \(T_1<T_2\) be maturities in years and \(r_{T_1},r_{T_2}\) the respective annual effective spot yields. Then

\[P_{T_1}=\frac{M}{(1+r_{T_1})^{T_1}},\qquad P_{T_2}=\frac{M}{(1+r_{T_2})^{T_2}}.\]

These are compound-price definitions for the stated yields, not the simple-interest model from the currency slide. Let \(F_{T_2}^{T_1}\) be today's agreed price for delivery of the later bond at \(T_1\), and \(f_{T_1,T_2}\) the annualized forward yield over \([T_1,T_2]\). At the earlier date the later bond has \(T_2-T_1\) years remaining, so

\[F_{T_2}^{T_1}=\frac{M}{(1+f_{T_1,T_2})^{T_2-T_1}}.\]

The forward rate is contracted/implied today. It is distinct from the as-yet-unknown spot yield that may prevail at \(T_1\). Treat the bonds as otherwise comparable and free of default risk in this idealized replication. L12(CostOfCarryModel).pptx, physical slide 9

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Deriving the forward-rate identity; fingerprint d7ab9842da46a637253eee946ddc40c7fda3e5255580ef0b62c78c83b2ff16d4. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Deriving the forward-rate identity

Today issue one earlier bond, receiving \(P_{T_1}\) and committing to repay \(M\) at \(T_1\). Spend those proceeds on \(q=P_{T_1}/P_{T_2}\) units of the later bond, and sell those units forward for delivery at \(T_1\). Opening net investment is zero. At \(T_1\) receive \(qF_{T_2}^{T_1}\) under the forward and repay \(M\). No arbitrage gives

\[qF_{T_2}^{T_1}=M,\qquad F_{T_2}^{T_1}=M\frac{P_{T_2}}{P_{T_1}}.\]

Insert the price formulas and cancel \(M\):

\[\frac{M}{(1+f_{T_1,T_2})^{T_2-T_1}} =M\frac{(1+r_{T_1})^{T_1}}{(1+r_{T_2})^{T_2}},\]

\[\boxed{(1+r_{T_2})^{T_2}=(1+r_{T_1})^{T_1}(1+f_{T_1,T_2})^{T_2-T_1}}.\]

The left side is growth over the full \(T_2\) years. The right side grows first to \(T_1\), then across the remaining interval at a rate locked today. Consequently

\[f_{T_1,T_2}=\left[\frac{(1+r_{T_2})^{T_2}}{(1+r_{T_1})^{T_1}}\right]^{1/(T_2-T_1)}-1.\]

This multiplication of growth factors is why merely subtracting spot yields does not compute the forward rate. It also explains the prerequisite: understand discounting and match dates before using a yield curve. No claim that the implied forward rate predicts the actual future rate follows from the replication. L12(CostOfCarryModel).pptx, physical slide 9

The source's timeline ends at the earlier maturity, because the later bond is sold forward then; there is no need to wait for its final face-value payment to settle this package. L12(CostOfCarryModel).pptx, physical slide 9

O018-I1

O018-I1, item_version 1, full_capability_check. Prompt: Comparable default-free zero-coupon bonds each pay face \(M=1000\), at \(T_1=2\) and \(T_2=3\) years. Annual effective spot yields are \(r_{T_1}=0.025\) and \(r_{T_2}=0.04\). Matching issue/purchase/forward transactions are possible. Compute both cash prices. Construct a zero-net-opening-investment package issuing one earlier bond and buying/selling forward the correct number of later bonds for delivery at \(T_1\). Derive the forward delivery price and the annual effective forward yield; show cash cancellation at both dates. Explain why subtracting spot yields, using the full \(T_2\) as forward duration, or interpreting the forward yield as a guaranteed future spot yield is invalid.

Complete solution and essential rubric: \(P_{T_1}=M/(1+r_{T_1})^{T_1}=951.81439619\) and \(P_{T_2}=M/(1+r_{T_2})^{T_2}=888.99635867\). Issue one earlier bond for \(P_{T_1}\), buy \(q=P_{T_1}/P_{T_2}=1.07066175\) later bonds and short \(q\) matching forwards. Opening cash \(P_{T_1}-qP_{T_2}=0\). At \(T_1\) deliver those later bonds and receive \(qF_{T_2}^{T_1}\), repaying face \(M\). Zero profit gives \(qF=M\) and \(F=M P_{T_2}/P_{T_1}=934.00179933\). With remaining life \(T_2-T_1=1\), \(F=M/(1+f_{T_1,T_2})^{T_2-T_1}\).
